children.top_down_role: Structural forms that expose independent cone blocks, linking structure, replicated decisions, or nested coupling.

assumptions_latex: \(I=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) is finite.
Each \(E_i\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Cartesian products of closed convex cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37
source_refs.source_title: Handbook of Semidefinite Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E=\prod_{i\in I}E_i\) carry the product inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_i\). The product-cone block geometry is the cone \[K:=\prod_{i\in I}K_i=\{x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\in E:x_i\in K_i\text{ for every }i\in I\}.\] Membership and projection are blockwise: \(x\in K\) exactly when every \(x_i\in K_i\), and \(P_K(x)=(P_{K_i}(x_i))_{i\in I}\). Its dual under the product inner product is \(K^*=\prod_{i\in I}K_i^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A product cone consists of independently constrained cone blocks; membership, Euclidean projection, and dualization operate block by block.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Block Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 The geometry of cone-lp's: main results p. 37
source_witnesses.source_title: Handbook of Semidefinite Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry of a finite Cartesian product of closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\prod_{i\in I}K_i\). Then \[\operatorname{ri}K=\prod_i\operatorname{ri}K_i,\qquad \operatorname{int}K=\prod_i\operatorname{int}K_i,\qquad \operatorname{lin}K=\prod_i\operatorname{lin}K_i.\] Every face of \(K\) is uniquely \(\prod_iF_i\) for faces \(F_i\unlhd K_i\), and it is exposed exactly when every \(F_i\) is exposed. Hence \(K\) is pointed, full-dimensional, or proper exactly when every factor has the corresponding property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interiors, interiors, lineality spaces, faces, exposed faces, and basic regularity properties of a finite product cone factor blockwise.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
Each \(K_i\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
Proper means closed, convex, pointed, and full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated interior, lineality, facial, exposedness, pointedness, full-dimensionality, and properness properties are determined factorwise.

notation.meaning: A face of the factor cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorwise Facial and Regularity Geometry

children.title: Separable Objective Structure
children.top_down_role: Objective decompositions indexed by blocks, scenarios, or local components.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite block index set.
For each \(i\in I\), \(X_i\) is a real vector space and \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive separability over the decision blocks.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the product space \(X:=\prod_{i\in I}X_i\), an objective has separable block structure when there exist local extended-real functions \(f_i\) such that \[f(x)=\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i)\qquad\text{for every }x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\in X.\] Thus changing block \(x_i\) while holding the other blocks fixed changes only the summand \(f_i(x_i)\). In the linear conic case, \(f_i(x_i)=\langle c_i,x_i\rangle\), so \(f(x)=\langle c,x\rangle\) with \(c=(c_i)_{i\in I}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-separable objective is an additive sum of local objectives, each depending on exactly one decision block.
knowledge_statements.title: Separable Objective Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core convex-analytic operations on a finite block-separable objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\prod_iX_i\) have the product Hilbert norm and let \(f(x)=\sum_i f_i(x_i)\), where every \(f_i\) is proper, closed, and convex. Then \[f^*(y)=\sum_i f_i^*(y_i),\qquad \partial f(x)=\prod_i\partial f_i(x_i),\] and for every \(\lambda>0\), \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x)=\bigl(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f_i}(x_i)\bigr)_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate, subdifferential, and proximal map of a proper closed convex separable objective factor blockwise.
assumptions_latex: The block index set is finite.
Each block is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
Every \(f_i\) is proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\), and the proximal map uses the product Hilbert norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^*=\sum_i f_i^*\), \(\partial f=\prod_i\partial f_i\), and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}\) acts blockwise.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the global objective.
Proximal mapping in the product Hilbert norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate, Subdifferential, and Proximal Factorization

children.title: Local Conic Systems
children.top_down_role: Block-specific conic constraints, variables, cone types, and local feasibility domains.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set.
For every \(i\in I\), \(X_i\) and \(Y_i\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces, \(A_i:X_i\to Y_i\) is linear, \(b_i\in Y_i\), and \(K_i\subseteq Y_i\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax-b\in K\) if and only if \(A_ix_i-b_i\in K_i\) for every \(i\in I\), and \(F=\prod_{i\in I}F_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent affine conic systems indexed by finitely many blocks.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X:=\prod_{i\in I}X_i\), \(Y:=\prod_{i\in I}Y_i\), \(A:=\operatorname{diag}(A_i)_{i\in I}:X\to Y\), \(b:=(b_i)_{i\in I}\), and \(K:=\prod_{i\in I}K_i\). A family of local conic systems consists of the block constraints \[A_ix_i-b_i\in K_i\qquad(i\in I).\] The family is equivalently represented by \[Ax-b\in K.\] Its feasible set is \(F=prod_{i\in I}F_i\), where \(F_i:=\{x_i\in X_i:A_ix_i-b_i\in K_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local conic systems constrain each decision block independently and combine into a block-diagonal conic system whose feasible set is the product of the local feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Conic Systems

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility regularity of an independent finite family of affine conic systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F_i=\{x_i:A_ix_i-b_i\in K_i\}\), the aggregate system is feasible exactly when every \(F_i\) is nonempty. Moreover, \[\exists x\ \forall i:\ A_ix_i-b_i\in\operatorname{int}K_i \iff \forall i\ \exists x_i:\ A_ix_i-b_i\in\operatorname{int}K_i.\] The same equivalence holds with \(\operatorname{ri}K_i\) for relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent aggregate conic system is feasible, strictly feasible, or relatively strictly feasible exactly when every local system has the corresponding property.
assumptions_latex: The block index set is finite.
Each variable block occurs only in its matching local system.
Each \(K_i\) is a nonempty convex cone; ambient strict feasibility requires nonempty \(\operatorname{int}K_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregate feasibility and both forms of strict feasibility are equivalent to their blockwise counterparts.

notation.meaning: Relative interior of the local cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Feasibility and Strict Feasibility

children.title: Objective-System Block Alignment
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between objective partitions and the partitions of local conic systems.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set and \(X=\prod_{j\in I}X_j\).
For every \(i,j\in I\), \(A_{ij}:X_j\to Y_i\) is linear; also \(b_i\in Y_i\) and \(K_i\subseteq Y_i\) is a closed convex cone.
The objective is a function \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective and system are block aligned when there are functions \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(f(x)=\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i)\) and \(A_{ij}=0\) for all \(i\ne j\).

notation.meaning: Operator block from decision block j to conic-system block i.
Local objective on decision block i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact matching between objective blocks and local-system blocks.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the block conic system \[\sum_{j\in I}A_{ij}x_j-b_i\in K_i\qquad(i\in I).\] Objective-system block alignment holds when the same partition \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\) separates both the objective and the conic system: there exist functions \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \[f(x)=\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i),\qquad A_{ij}=0\quad\text{whenever }i\ne j.\] Under this condition, each objective term and each conic-system block use only their matching decision block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-system block alignment means that one partition makes the objective additive by block and makes the conic-system operator block diagonal.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-System Block Alignment

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficiency and nonnecessity of the displayed common-partition alignment test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When the objective is additive and the displayed conic system is block diagonal for the same partition, its value separates as \[\inf_{x_i\in F_i}\sum_i f_i(x_i)=\sum_i\inf_{x_i\in F_i}f_i(x_i),\] whenever the finite extended-real sum is well defined; attained local minimizers concatenate to a global minimizer. If either condition is dropped, independent optimization has no general guarantee: for example, \(x_1+x_2=1\) couples feasibility, while a joint term such as \((x_1-x_2)^2\) couples the objective. Conversely, failure of the displayed zero-pattern test is not by itself proof of intrinsic nonseparability, because invertible row transformations, redundant equations, or a different valid partition may reveal a Cartesian system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common-partition alignment is sufficient for exact independent optimization; objective or feasibility coupling can destroy the guarantee, but a failed syntactic zero-pattern test need not prove intrinsic coupling.
assumptions_latex: The decision-space partition is fixed when applying the seed's alignment test.
The separated extended-real value sum is well defined.
Statements about concatenated minimizers require attainment of the relevant local infima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact displayed alignment guarantees value and minimizer separation, whereas its failure removes that guarantee without necessarily proving intrinsic nonseparability.
review_flags: Revised to avoid treating syntactic off-diagonal structure as a necessary characterization of intrinsic separability.
knowledge_statements.title: Alignment Guarantees and Their Boundary

children.title: Linking Constraints
children.top_down_role: Cross-block constraints that coordinate otherwise local conic systems.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite index set, and \(X_i\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces for every \(i\in I\).
For every \(i\in I\), \(L_i:X_i\to Y\) is linear; \(d\in Y\); and \(Q\subseteq Y\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in I}L_ix_i-d\in Q\), with \(L_i\ne0\) for at least two distinct indices, is a linking constraint for the block family.

notation.meaning: Contribution of block i to the linking relation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine conic relations structurally incident to multiple otherwise local variable blocks.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given otherwise local block systems, a linking constraint is an affine conic relation \[\sum_{i\in I}L_ix_i-d\in Q\] whose operator is incident to at least two variable blocks, meaning that \(L_i\ne0\) and \(L_j\ne0\) for some distinct \(i,j\in I\). The equality-linked case is obtained by taking \(Q=\{0\}\). With \(X:=\prod_{i\in I}X_i\) and \(L:X\to Y\) defined by \(Lx:=\sum_{i\in I}L_ix_i\), the linking constraint is \(Lx-d\in Q\). Removing this relation restores independence when all remaining constraints are local to individual blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linking constraint is an affine conic relation whose operator is incident to at least two otherwise local variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Linking Constraints

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86

children.title: Shared Variables
children.top_down_role: Variables represented across multiple blocks or local conic systems.

assumptions_latex: \(z\in Z\) is a global decision vector.
For each \(i\in I\), \(x_i\in X_i\) is a local decision vector.

notation.meaning: Variable used by multiple local systems.
Map from the shared-variable space into local system i.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global variables appearing in multiple local conic systems.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a block conic model with local variables \(x_i\), a shared variable is a vector \(z\in Z\) that enters more than one local system. A canonical representation is \[A_ix_i+B_iz-b_i\in K_i\qquad(i\in I),\] with \(B_i\ne0\) for at least two indices. The variable \(z\) is stored once and must take the same value in every incident system. Introducing local copies \(z_i\) gives an equivalent consensus formulation only when constraints enforcing \(z_i=z_j\) connect all copies that represent \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared variable is one global decision vector used by multiple local conic systems, equivalently representable by consistently linked local copies.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared Variables

children.title: Linking-Variable Incidence
children.top_down_role: Incidence patterns connecting shared variables to linking constraints and block models.

assumptions_latex: The block model has linking rows indexed by \(R\) and variable blocks indexed by \(I\).
\(L_{ri}:X_i\to Y_r\) denotes the corresponding operator block.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite support pattern of linking rows and variable blocks.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For linking relations \(\sum_{i\in I}L_{ri}x_i-d_r\in Q_r\) indexed by \(r\in R\), the linking-variable incidence is the bipartite graph \[G=(R\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E),\qquad E:=\{(r,i)\in R\times I:L_{ri}\ne0\}.\] Its biadjacency matrix \(H\in\{0,1\}^{R\times I}\) is given by \(H_{ri}=1\) exactly when \(L_{ri}\ne0\). Row degree counts blocks participating in a linking relation, while column degree counts linking relations incident to a variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linking-variable incidence is the bipartite support graph connecting each coupling row to every variable block with a nonzero operator block.
knowledge_statements.title: Linking-Variable Incidence

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of the incidence graph on the declared linking-row and cone-factor partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The incidence graph is relative to the chosen linking-row groups. Coarsening several independently factored conic relations into one row vertex can connect variable blocks that separate after the row space and cone are refined. For example, the single declared relation \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R_+^2\) has one row vertex incident to both blocks, yet it is equivalent to the independent relations \(x_1\in\mathbb R_+\) and \(x_2\in\mathbb R_+\). Consequently, disconnectedness certifies decomposition, whereas connectedness is not an invariant obstruction unless the row and cone-factor partition is fixed and irreducible for the intended representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence depends on row-group granularity: combining independent cone factors can create an apparently connected graph, so connectedness is not by itself a certificate of true coupling.
assumptions_latex: Incidence vertices represent declared linking-row groups rather than uniquely determined atomic relations.
Cone and row-space refinements are permitted when testing equivalent formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ connected does not imply algebraic indecomposability without a fixed suitable row partition}.
knowledge_statements.title: Incidence Granularity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural decomposition certified by disconnected linking incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume every objective term and nonlinking constraint is local to one variable block and every cross-block relation is represented by \(G=(R\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\). If \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) are the connected components of \(G\), then row and variable-block permutations separate the model into independent component subproblems. When their extended-real optimal values are well defined, \[\inf_x\sum_{i\in I}f_i(x_i)=\sum_{\ell=1}^q\inf_{(x_i)_{i\in C_\ell\cap I}}\sum_{i\in C_\ell\cap I}f_i(x_i),\] with the constraints assigned to the same components. This is a sufficient support certificate; connected incidence does not by itself prove algebraic indecomposability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disconnected incidence components certify independent subproblems when all nonlocal relations are represented, but connected incidence alone does not prove that a formulation cannot be refined or decomposed algebraically.
assumptions_latex: Every objective term and nonlinking constraint is local to one variable block.
Every cross-block relation is represented in \(G\).
Component infima are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ disconnected}\Longrightarrow\text{structural decomposition over the connected components of }G.

notation.meaning: connected component of the bipartite incidence graph

knowledge_statements.title: Incidence-Component Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-mode projection of linking-row incidence onto variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G=(R\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\), define \(G_I=(I,E_I)\) by \[\{i,j\}\in E_I\iff i\ne j\text{ and }\exists r\in R:\ (r,i),(r,j)\in E.\] If \(H\) is the biadjacency matrix, then \(\{i,j\}\in E_I\) exactly when \((H^\top H)_{ij}>0\). A linking-row vertex of degree \(d_r\) therefore induces a clique on its incident variable blocks in this projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two variable blocks are adjacent in the projected interaction graph exactly when they share a linking-row vertex; each such row induces a clique.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) and \(I\) are finite.
\(H_{ri}=1\) exactly when \(L_{ri}\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Block-Interaction Graph

children.title: Coupling Sparsity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Sparse, dense, hierarchical, and partially shared coupling structures.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(R\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\) is the linking-variable incidence graph.
A family size parameter \(n\) indexes the block models.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E|=O(|R|+|I|)\) under bounded incidence degree, whereas \(|E|=\Theta(|R||I|)\) in the dense regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic regimes defined by incidence-graph support growth.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of block models is in the bounded-incidence sparse regime when \(\sup_n\Delta(G_n)<\infty\), which implies \(|E_n|=O(|R_n|+|I_n|)\). More generally it is asymptotically sparse when \[|E_n|=o(|R_n||I_n|).\] It is dense when \(|E_n|=\Theta(|R_n||I_n|)\). An intermediate regime has unbounded degree but vanishing edge density. These conditions concern the support of coupling blocks; they do not require the nonzero operators \(L_{ri}\) themselves to be sparse internally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling sparsity is classified by incidence growth: bounded degree, vanishing edge density, intermediate growth, or a constant-order fraction of all possible links.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling Sparsity Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed graph bounds are plausible, but the proposed four-regime asymptotic classification is a noncanonical taxonomy and the cited broad structure-exploitation section has not been shown to support it. A source specifically defining or motivating these incidence-growth regimes is required before the mathematical version can be accepted.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
Each \(K_i\subseteq E_i\) is a closed convex cone, with no requirement that the cones share a type or dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\prod_{i\in I}K_i\) permits distinct cone families across blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product models whose component cones may belong to different families.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A heterogeneous cone-block model is a product-cone model \[K:=\prod_{i\in I}K_i\subseteq\prod_{i\in I}E_i\] in which the factors may have different dimensions, algebraic descriptions, or cone families. For example, distinct factors may be nonnegative orthants, second-order cones, or positive-semidefinite cones. Feasibility remains blockwise: \(x\in K\) if and only if \(x_i\in K_i\) for every \(i\). Under the product inner product, heterogeneity does not alter the dual-product identity \(K^*=\prod_{i\in I}K_i^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heterogeneous cone blocks form a product cone whose factors may have different dimensions and cone types while retaining blockwise membership and duality.
knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Cone Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

assumptions_latex: Each \(A_i:X_i\to Y_i\) defines a local block system.
\(L_i:X_i\to Y_0\) maps block variables into common linking rows.

notation.meaning: Block contribution to the common linking rows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal local rows augmented by common coupling rows.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A row-linked conic block structure has a block-diagonal collection of local constraint rows together with one or more row groups spanning several variable blocks. After suitable row and column permutations, its operator has the form \[\mathcal A=\begin{bmatrix}A_1&&0\\&\ddots&\\0&&A_p\\L_1&\cdots&L_p\end{bmatrix}.\] The rows containing \(A_i\) define local conic systems, whereas the final row group imposes \(\sum_{i=1}^pL_ix_i-d\in Q\). Deleting the final row group leaves a block-diagonal operator and independent local systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A row-linked structure adds common coupling rows beneath block-diagonal local constraint rows; removing those rows separates the blocks.
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Linked Conic Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(z\in Z\) is a shared variable block.
Each local system has private variables \(x_i\in X_i\) and operators \(A_i:X_i\to Y_i\), \(B_i:Z\to Y_i\).

notation.meaning: Local action of the shared variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-diagonal private columns augmented by shared-variable columns.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A column-linked conic block structure has private variable columns that are block diagonal and an additional shared column block entering multiple local row groups. After suitable permutations, its operator is \[\mathcal A=\begin{bmatrix}A_1&&0&B_1\\&\ddots&&\vdots\\0&&A_p&B_p\end{bmatrix},\] representing constraints \(A_ix_i+B_iz-b_i\in K_i\). At least two maps \(B_i\) are nonzero. Fixing or deleting the shared variable \(z\) leaves independent local systems in the private variables \(x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column-linked structure appends shared-variable columns to otherwise block-diagonal private columns, causing the shared variables to enter multiple local systems.
knowledge_statements.title: Column-Linked Conic Blocks

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

assumptions_latex: \(T=(V,E)\) is a rooted tree of block groups.
Each node \(v\in V\) has local variables \(x_v\), local conic rows, and possible links to its ancestors or children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_v=\operatorname{diag}(\mathcal A_c)_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}+\mathcal L_v\) recursively describes the hierarchy.

notation.meaning: Linking operator introduced at node v.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive block-angular structure indexed by a rooted decomposition tree.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Special Cases and Structure Exploitation p. 86

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nested block-angular conic structure is indexed by a rooted tree \(T\). At every nonleaf node \(v\), the operator for its subtree consists of the block-diagonal child operators plus row-linking or column-linking blocks introduced at \(v\): \[\mathcal A_v=\operatorname{diag}(\mathcal A_c)_{c\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}+\mathcal L_v.\] Each leaf supplies a local conic system. The support of \(\mathcal L_v\) is confined to variables or rows belonging to the subtree rooted at \(v\). Removing all linking blocks at a fixed level separates the descendant subtrees below that level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested block-angular model recursively combines child block systems and level-specific links along a rooted tree; deleting one level's links separates descendant subtrees.
knowledge_statements.title: Nested Block-Angular Conic Structures

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling constraints whose relaxation or deletion exposes independent conic blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a variable partition \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\) and a separable core \(x_i\in F_i\). A designated constraint family \[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\] is a complicating constraint family when removing or relaxing that family leaves the Cartesian feasible set \(\prod_iF_i\), and the family is incident to at least two blocks after redundant rows are removed. The notion is relative to the chosen partition and retained constraints. A syntactically cross-block row is not genuine evidence of complication when it is redundant; conversely, retained cross-block constraints prevent the residual problem from being a product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complicating constraints are nonredundant coupling rows whose removal or relaxation exposes a Cartesian product of independent block systems.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) and all spaces are finite-dimensional.
The block partition and retained local systems \(F_i\) are fixed.
Redundant coupling rows are removed when classifying genuine structural coupling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deleting or relaxing the designated nonredundant coupling family leaves \(\prod_iF_i\); retaining genuine cross-block rows generally destroys that product structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Complicating Constraint Family
Complicating Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coupling rows whose removal separates a block-structured conic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider blocks \(x_i\in K_i\) with local equations \(B_i x_i=d_i\). A family of constraints is complicating when it has the form
\[\sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\]
and deleting this family makes the feasible region equal to the Cartesian product
\[\prod_{i=1}^m\{x_i\in K_i:B_i x_i=d_i\}.\]
Thus each retained block can be optimized independently once the common constraint is removed or suitably coordinated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complicating constraints are coupling rows whose deletion leaves independent conic subproblems, one for each variable block.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 2\) and each \(K_i\) is a convex cone.
All displayed linear maps have compatible finite-dimensional domains and codomains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:B_i x_i=d_i,\ x_i\in K_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is block-separable after removing \(\sum_i A_i x_i=b\).

notation.meaning: map from block i into the coupling space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared variables whose fixation leaves independent local optimization blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a model with a shared block \(z\), local blocks \(x_i\), conditionally additive objective \[f_0(z)+\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i;z),\] and constraints \(x_i\in F_i(z)\). The block \(z\) is a complicating variable relative to this representation when it enters at least two local components and, for every fixed value \(\bar z\) under consideration, the residual feasible set is \[\prod_{i=1}^mF_i(\bar z)\] and the residual objective remains additive in the \(x_i\). Fixing \(z=\bar z\) therefore yields independent block subproblems. A merely shared variable is not complicating in this sense if residual cross-block constraints or objective terms remain after it is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complicating variable is shared across components and fixing it makes both the residual feasible set and residual objective block separable.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\), and the representation and variable partition are fixed.
The quantifier ranges over fixed values for which the residual extended-real model is defined.
No residual cross-block term is hidden inside a local set or objective term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixing the complicating variable produces independent block problems; sharing alone is insufficient if residual coupling remains.

notation.meaning: Local feasible fiber after fixing \(z=\bar z\).

review_flags: Strengthens the deferred feasible-fiber candidate by also requiring conditional objective separability.
The classification is explicitly relative to the displayed representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Complicating Variable by Conditional Separation
Complicating Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines shared variables whose fixation separates the remaining conic blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the feasible set be
\[X=\{(z,x_1,\ldots,x_m):x_i\in K_i,\ B_i x_i+C_i z=d_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
The variable \(z\) is complicating if, for every fixed admissible value \(\bar z\), its fiber factors as
\[X(\bar z)=\prod_{i=1}^m\{x_i\in K_i:B_i x_i=d_i-C_i\bar z\}.\]
Consequently, fixing \(z\) leaves independent block subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complicating variable is shared across blocks, while fixing its value makes the residual feasible set a Cartesian product of independent conic fibers.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge 2\) and each \(K_i\) is a convex cone.
The constraints contain no cross-block terms other than dependence on \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X(\bar z)\) is a Cartesian product for every admissible \(\bar z\).

notation.meaning: feasible fiber obtained by fixing z

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports this decomposition definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fiber-factorization definition is coherent and locally appropriate, but it has no supporting citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-level cone-map coupling relative to prescribed domain and range blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix domain blocks \(X=\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\), range blocks \(Y=\prod_{r=1}^qY_r\), and a cone product \(Q=\prod_{r=1}^qQ_r\). An affine cone map \(H:X\to Y\), with components \(H_r\), is block separable relative to these partitions if the range blocks can be assigned to domain blocks so that each \(H_r(x)\) depends on only its assigned \(x_i\). The cone membership \(H(x)\in Q\) then becomes independent block memberships. A map is complicating relative to the prescribed representation when no such assignment exists after deleting constant or redundant range blocks. This classification is representation-dependent: a change of coordinates, cone isomorphism, repartition, or lift may expose a separable representation even when the displayed map is complicating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complicating cone map has genuine cross-block incidence in a prescribed product-cone representation, although reformulation or repartitioning can change that classification.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional.
The domain partition, range partition, and product decomposition of \(Q\) are fixed for the test.
Redundant range blocks are removed before declaring genuine coupling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Block separability is equivalent to assigning each nonredundant cone-membership component to one domain block; failure of this test makes the displayed cone map complicating, but not invariantly so under reformulation.

notation.meaning: Range-block component of the affine cone map.
Prescribed product decomposition of the range cone.

review_flags: Replaces the deferred candidate's unspecified equivalence notion with an explicit representation-relative definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition-Relative Complicating Cone Map
Complicating Cone Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines conic maps that prevent product-cone separation across variable blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For block variables \(x_i\in E_i\), consider the conic constraint
\[h-\sum_{i=1}^m G_i x_i\in Q.\]
Its aggregate map \(G(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_iG_i x_i\) is a complicating cone map relative to the chosen blocks when this membership condition cannot be written as independent conditions \(h_i-G_i'x_i\in Q_i\) with \(Q=\prod_iQ_i\). Removing, splitting, or coordinating this map restores product-cone subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complicating cone map sends several variable blocks into one nonseparable cone constraint, preventing a product of independent conic subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \(E_i\) and the range of \(G\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(Q\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is complicating precisely when the displayed cone membership lacks a blockwise product-cone representation for the selected partition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-master optimality test for a restricted generator master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_v\lambda_v:\sum_{v\in V}a_v\lambda_v=b,\ \lambda_v\ge0\right\}.\] Let \(\bar\lambda\) and \(y^k\) be optimal restricted-master primal and dual solutions over \(V^k\subseteq V\). If \(r_v^k=c_v-\langle a_v,y^k\rangle\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\), then \(y^k\) is full-dual feasible and \(\bar\lambda\), extended by zero, is full-master optimal. A missing generator with \(r_v^k<0\) certifies failure of full-dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative reduced costs for all generators certify full-master optimality; a negative reduced cost identifies a missing improving column candidate.
assumptions_latex: The restricted primal and dual have equal attained finite values.
Master solutions use finite-support coefficient vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-addition bound under exact nondeleting generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(V\) is finite, pricing is exact, every nonterminal iteration adds a previously absent negative-reduced-cost generator, and columns are never deleted, then termination occurs after at most \(|V\setminus V^0|\) column-adding iterations, at which point the pricing optimality certificate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact nonrepeating column generation over a finite generator set adds at most all initially absent columns.
assumptions_latex: \(|V|<\infty\).
Pricing detects a missing negative-reduced-cost generator whenever one exists.
Columns are neither repeated nor deleted.
review_flags: The bound counts column-adding iterations, not master resolves or oracle work.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Generator Termination Bound
Primal Generation Orientation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted-master representation underlying primal column or atom generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each block satisfy \(x_i\in\operatorname{cone}(V_i)\), where \(V_i\) is a set of feasible generators. Writing
\[x_i=\sum_{v\in V_i}\lambda_{iv}v,\qquad \lambda_{iv}\ge0,\]
transfers coupling constraints to a master problem in the coefficients \(\lambda_{iv}\). Replacing \(V_i\) by finite subsets \(V_i^k\) yields a restricted primal master. A primal-generation orientation enlarges \(V_i^k\) using blockwise pricing or separation until no generator improves the master under its dual prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal generation solves a restricted master over block generators and repeatedly adds blockwise atoms identified by pricing.
assumptions_latex: Each block-feasible cone is generated by the stated set \(V_i\).
Restricted masters and block pricing problems attain the values used by the procedure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\in\operatorname{cone}(V_i)\) is represented by nonnegative generator coefficients, with finite subsets producing restricted primal masters.
review_flags: A source for the intended conic column-generation formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits primal generation, but the conic column-generation formulation and its stopping interpretation lack a source; the intended finite-support meaning of the generator sum also needs confirmation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity, exactness, and attainment boundaries for dual projection cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi(z)\) be a primal block value and \(d(z)=\sup_{y\in Y}\ell_y(z)\) its dual value, with each \(\ell_y\) affine. Weak duality gives \(\ell_y(z)\le d(z)\le\phi(z)\). Thus every dual-feasible \(y\) gives a valid lower cut. The dual envelope equals \(\phi\) exactly where the duality gap is zero. A cut touching \(\phi\) at a sampled parameter additionally requires attainment of the dual supremum there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility gives valid cuts, zero gap gives an exact cut envelope, and dual attainment gives a touching cut.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual values are interpreted in the extended-real sense.
Each \(\ell_y\) is generated by a dual-feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_y\le d\le\phi;\quad d(z)=\phi(z)\text{ gives envelope exactness, while attained }d(z)\text{ gives a touching cut}.

notation.meaning: affine cut generated by dual-feasible y

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Envelope Exactness Boundary
Dual Projection Orientation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cut representation obtained by projecting local conic variables from a coupled model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameter \(z\), define the block value
\[\phi_i(z)=\inf\{\langle c_i,x_i\rangle:B_i x_i=d_i-C_i z,\ x_i\in K_i\}.\]
If conic strong duality holds for this block, then
\[\phi_i(z)=\sup\{\langle d_i-C_i z,y_i\rangle:B_i^*y_i+s_i=c_i,\ s_i\in K_i^*\}.\]
Hence projecting out \(x_i\) represents the epigraph of \(\phi_i\) by affine inequalities indexed by dual-feasible \((y_i,s_i)\). Dual projection iteratively adds violated inequalities to a master problem in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual projection eliminates local primal blocks and represents their value functions by cuts indexed by dual-feasible conic certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\) is a closed convex cone.
For every parameter considered, the block primal-dual pair has zero gap and the required optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\phi_i\) equals the intersection of the affine epigraph halfspaces generated by all dual-feasible \((y_i,s_i)\).

notation.meaning: dual cone of the local cone

review_flags: The supplied primal-dual locators do not specifically certify this projection-and-cut formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conic dual projection formula is plausible under the stated strong-duality assumptions, but no cited locator supports the projection-and-cut representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orientation principle that places coupling relations in a Lagrangian multiplier master and retains separable block subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a separable core \(x_i\in X_i\), objective \(\sum_i f_i(x_i)\), and coupling equation \(\sum_iA_ix_i=b\), the coupling-relaxation orientation dualizes the coupling equation and uses its multiplier \(y\) as the master coordinate. Its evaluation has the block form \[g(y)=-\langle b,y\rangle+\sum_i\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_ix_i,y\rangle\bigr).\] Every defined value \(g(y)\) is a primal lower bound. This orientation decomposes only when all retained terms separate after dualization; zero duality gap and dual attainment are not implied by the orientation and require the regularity conditions stated in the canonical linking-constraint relaxation theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling relaxation puts linking multipliers in a master problem and evaluates the dual bound through independent local Lagrangian subproblems; strong duality is a separate regularity result.
assumptions_latex: The primal is a finite-dimensional convex minimization problem with a separable retained core.
The relaxed coupling relation is affine.
Each block infimum is interpreted in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier master has a separable dual-value evaluation and supplies weak-duality lower bounds, while decomposition and strong duality require separate structural and regularity conditions.

notation.meaning: Multiplier and master coordinate for the relaxed coupling equation.

review_flags: Restricted to the orientation principle; the full strong-duality theorem and oracle algorithm remain at their canonical nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Master Coupling-Relaxation Orientation
Coupling-Relaxation Orientation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lagrangian decomposition obtained by dualizing block-coupling equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[p^*=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i):x_i\in X_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m A_i x_i=b\right\},\]
relax the coupling equation with multiplier \(y\). The Lagrangian dual function separates:
\[g(y)=-\langle b,y\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^m\inf_{x_i\in X_i}\bigl(f_i(x_i)+\langle A_i x_i,y\rangle\bigr).\]
The coupling-relaxation orientation maximizes \(g(y)\); each evaluation is performed by independent block subproblems. Weak duality gives \(g(y)\le p^*\), with equality under an applicable conic constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling relaxation dualizes linking equations, producing a multiplier master whose objective is the sum of independent block value functions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(X_i\) is nonempty and each block infimum is well-defined in the extended-real sense.
The primal problem is a convex conic optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y g(y)\le p^*\), and equality holds whenever conic strong duality applies.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically addresses Lagrangian coupling relaxation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separable Lagrangian relaxation is standard and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Scenario-Consensus Orientation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scenario decomposition using local copies tied to a common consensus variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given scenario functions \(f_s\), sets \(X_s\), and weights \(p_s\ge0\) with \(\sum_s p_s=1\), the common-decision problem
\[\inf_{z\in\bigcap_s X_s}\sum_s p_s f_s(z)\]
has the consensus representation
\[\inf_{z,\{x_s\}}\left\{\sum_s p_s f_s(x_s):x_s\in X_s,\ x_s=z\text{ for every }s\right\}.\]
Relaxing or splitting the equalities \(x_s=z\) makes the scenario subproblems separable; coordination updates enforce consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scenario-consensus decomposition duplicates the common decision by scenario and couples the copies only through equalities requiring agreement with one consensus variable.
assumptions_latex: The scenario index set is finite.
Every \(X_s\) is a convex conic-representable set and every \(f_s\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The common-decision and consensus formulations have identical feasible decisions and identical optimal values.

notation.meaning: local decision copy for scenario s

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports scenario-consensus decomposition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consensus reformulation is mathematically coherent and correctly classified as a representation, but no citation supports its placement and formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: General Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definition of a face of a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space. A convex cone \(F\subseteq K\) is a face of \(K\), written \(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\), if
\[u,v\in K,\quad u+v\in F\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u,v\in F.\]
Equivalently, whenever a relative-interior point of a line segment contained in \(K\) lies in \(F\), both endpoints lie in \(F\). The cone \(K\) itself is always a face, and \(\{0\}\) is a face exactly when \(K\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone face is a convex subcone that contains both conic summands whenever it contains their sum.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\) if and only if, for all \(u,v\in K\), the inclusion \(u+v\in F\) implies \(u,v\in F\).

notation.meaning: F is a face of K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exposed faces of products of second-order and semidefinite cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States product factorization and orthogonal-automorphism equivariance for faces exposed in an SOC/PSD product cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal K=\prod_{i=1}^q\mathcal K_i\), where every \(\mathcal K_i\) is a second-order or semidefinite cone, and let \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_q)\in\mathcal K\). Define \(\operatorname{face}(\mathcal K,z)=\{x\in\mathcal K:z^Tx=0\}\). Since \(x_i^Tz_i\ge0\) for \(x_i,z_i\in\mathcal K_i\), \(\operatorname{face}(\mathcal K,z)=\prod_{i=1}^q\operatorname{face}(\mathcal K_i,z_i)\). For \(Q\in\operatorname{OAut}(\mathcal K_i)\), \(Q\operatorname{face}(\mathcal K_i,z_i)=\operatorname{face}(\mathcal K_i,Qz_i)\). Orthogonal cone automorphisms can place SOC exposing vectors in spectral coordinates and PSD exposing matrices in nonnegative diagonal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face exposed in a product of SOC and PSD cones is the product of the corresponding exposed block faces. Orthogonal cone automorphisms preserve this construction and can place exposing vectors in spectral or diagonal form.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines faces cut out by supporting hyperplanes through the cone apex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let
\[K^*=\{y:\langle y,x\rangle\ge0\text{ for every }x\in K\}.\]
A face \(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\) is exposed if there exists \(y\in K^*\) such that
\[F=K\cap y^\perp=\{x\in K:\langle y,x\rangle=0\}.\]
The vector \(y\) exposes \(F\). Thus an exposed face is exactly the minimizer set over \(K\) of a nonnegative linear functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed cone face is the intersection of the cone with the zero hyperplane of some functional in the dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is exposed if and only if \(F=K\cap y^\perp\) for some \(y\in K^*\).

notation.meaning: zero hyperplane of the functional induced by y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-cone characterization of exposed faces and their exact exposing vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a face \(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\), define \(F^\triangle:=K^*\cap F^\perp\). Then
\[
F\text{ is exposed}\iff F=K\cap(F^\triangle)^\perp.
\]
When \(F\) is exposed, \(y\in K^*\) exposes exactly \(F\) if and only if \(y\in\operatorname{ri}(F^\triangle)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is exposed exactly when conjugation to the dual cone and back returns it; the relative interior of its conjugate face is precisely the set of vectors exposing it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(F\) is a face of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is exposed}\iff F=K\cap(F^\triangle)^\perp\), and then \(\{y\in K^*:K\cap y^\perp=F\}=\operatorname{ri}(F^\triangle)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Face Characterization of Exposure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Intersections of Exposed Cone Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of exposed faces under finite intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F_i=K\cap y_i^\perp\) with \(y_i\in K^*\), then
\[

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed-Face Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies where single supporting-hyperplane facial reduction ceases to represent every face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\). The face \(F\) is nonexposed precisely when
\[F\ne K\cap y^\perp\qquad\text{for every }y\in K^*.\]
Equivalently, no single nonnegative linear functional has exactly \(F\) as its zero set on \(K\). Consequently, arguments that identify every target face using one exposing vector apply only when the relevant faces are exposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed face cannot be isolated by one dual supporting hyperplane, marking the limit of one-step exposure-based facial reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(F\mathrel{\unlhd}K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonexposed if and only if no \(y\in K^*\) satisfies \(F=K\cap y^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Exposure Hierarchies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents nested facial reduction as successive exposures inside current faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exposure hierarchy in a closed convex cone \(K\) is a strict chain
\[K=F_0\supsetneq F_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq F_r\]
for which, at every level \(j\), there exists \(y_j\in F_{j-1}^*\) satisfying
\[F_j=F_{j-1}\cap y_j^\perp.\]
Each step exposes \(F_j\) relative to the current face, even when the final face need not be exposed directly in \(K\). The least possible length \(r\) for a target face is its exposure-chain depth under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face-exposure hierarchy reaches a target face through nested faces, each exposed by one functional relative to its immediate predecessor.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
Every \(F_j\) in the chain is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_r\) is obtained from \(K\) by \(r\) successive relative-exposure operations.

notation.meaning: dual cone of the current face in its span

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Faces of Conic Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smallest cone face containing all feasible conic slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear, let \(b\in Y\), and let \(K\subseteq Y\) be a closed convex cone. Suppose the conic system \(b-Ax\in K\) has the nonempty slack set
\[S=\{b-Ax:x\in E,\ b-Ax\in K\}.\]
Its minimal face in \(K\) is
\[F_{\min}=\bigcap\{F:F\mathrel{\unlhd}K,\ S\subseteq F\}.\]
This intersection is a face, contains every feasible slack, and is contained in every face containing \(S\). Moreover,
\[S\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_{\min})\ne\varnothing.\]
Thus replacing \(K\) by \(F_{\min}\) preserves the feasible set and gives a feasible slack in the relative interior of the reduced cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimal face of a feasible conic system is the smallest face containing every feasible slack; replacing the original cone by that face preserves feasibility and yields relative strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(A:E\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone.
The slack set \(S\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\min}\) is the unique smallest face of \(K\) containing \(S\), and \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_{\min})\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: minimal face containing the slack set

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal cone face containing all feasible primal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and consider the nonempty primal feasible set
\[P=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}.\]
Its primal minimal face is
\[F_P:=\bigcap\{F:F\unlhd K,\ P\subseteq F\}=\operatorname{face}_K(P).\]
Equivalently, \(F_P\) is the unique face of \(K\) such that \(P\subseteq F_P\), \(P\cap\operatorname{ri}F_P\neq\varnothing\), and no proper face of \(F_P\) contains \(P\). The reduced primal feasibility system is \(Ax=b\), \(x\in F_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal minimal face is the unique smallest face of the primal cone containing every feasible variable; the feasible set meets its relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space.
\(P=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_P=\operatorname{face}_K(P)\) is the unique minimal face containing \(P\), and \(P\cap\operatorname{ri}F_P\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Minimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal dual-cone face containing all feasible dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K^*\subseteq E\) be the dual of a closed convex cone \(K\), and consider the nonempty dual-slack set
\[D=K^*\cap\{c-A^*y:y\in\mathbb R^m\}.\]
Its dual minimal face is
\[F_D:=\bigcap\{G:G\unlhd K^*,\ D\subseteq G\}=\operatorname{face}_{K^*}(D).\]
Equivalently, \(F_D\) is the unique face of \(K^*\) satisfying \(D\subseteq F_D\), \(D\cap\operatorname{ri}F_D\neq\varnothing\), and minimality under face inclusion. Replacing \(s\in K^*\) by \(s\in F_D\) preserves precisely the feasible dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual minimal face is the unique smallest face of the dual cone containing all feasible dual slacks, and those slacks meet its relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(D=K^*\cap(c-\operatorname{range}A^*)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D=\operatorname{face}_{K^*}(D)\) is the unique minimal face containing \(D\), and \(D\cap\operatorname{ri}F_D\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-face inclusions induced by complementary primal and dual solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq K\) and \(S\subseteq K^*\) be nonempty convex sets satisfying \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(s\in S\). Let \(F_P=\operatorname{face}_K(X)\) and \(F_D=\operatorname{face}_{K^*}(S)\). For a face \(F\unlhd K\), define its conjugate face by \(F^\triangle=K^*\cap F^\perp\), and analogously for faces of \(K^*\). Then
\[F_D\subseteq F_P^\triangle\quad\text{and}\quad F_P\subseteq F_D^\triangle.\]
If relatively interior points \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F_P\) and \(\bar s\in\operatorname{ri}F_D\) satisfy \(F_D=K^*\cap\bar x^\perp\) and \(F_P=K\cap\bar s^\perp\), the pairing is exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity places each minimal face inside the conjugate of the other. Equality requires an exact complementary-face pairing, such as that induced by suitable relative-interior solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(X\subseteq K\) and \(S\subseteq K^*\) are nonempty convex sets.
\(\langle x,s\rangle=0\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(s\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D\subseteq F_P^\triangle\) and \(F_P\subseteq F_D^\triangle\); under the stated exposure equalities, both inclusions are equalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Mismatched Minimal-Face Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity alone does not force conjugate primal-dual minimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=K^*=\mathbb R_+^2\), let \(e_1=(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\), and take the complementary convex sets \(X=\{e_1\}\subseteq K\) and \(S=\{0\}\subseteq K^*\). Their minimal faces are
\[F_P=\mathbb R_+e_1,\qquad F_D=\{0\}.\]
Although \(\langle x,s\rangle=0\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(s\in S\), their conjugate faces satisfy
\[F_P^\triangle=\mathbb R_+e_2\neq F_D,\qquad F_D^\triangle=K\neq F_P.\]
Thus complementarity yields only conjugate-face inclusions; equality can fail when one side lacks a relatively interior complementary point exposing the other side's minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary primal and dual sets can generate nonconjugate minimal faces. A two-dimensional orthant example shows that complementarity alone is insufficient for exact face pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\) with the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_D\subsetneq F_P^\triangle\) and \(F_P\subsetneq F_D^\triangle\), despite universal complementarity between \(X\) and \(S\).

notation.meaning: The standard coordinate vectors (1,0) and (0,1), respectively.

Exposing-Vector Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step facial-reduction certificate for a primal conic feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and define \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\). A vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is an exposing-vector certificate if
\[z=A^*y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle=0.\]
Then
\[S\subseteq K\cap z^\perp,\]
and \(K\cap z^\perp\) is a proper exposed face of \(K\). Thus the verifiable data \((y,z)\) certify that replacing \(K\) by \(K\cap z^\perp\) preserves the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier whose adjoint image is a dual-cone vector that does not annihilate the cone, and which is orthogonal to the right-hand side, certifies a proper exposed face containing every feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Theorems of Alternatives for Face Exposure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible conic alternative separating relative Slater points from exposing multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and suppose \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Exactly one of the following systems holds:
\[(i)\quad Ax=b\ \text{for some }x\in\operatorname{ri}K;\]
\[(ii)\quad A^*y\in K^*\setminus K^\perp,\quad \langle b,y\rangle=0\ \text{for some }y\in\mathbb R^m.\]
When \((ii)\) holds, \(K\cap(A^*y)^\perp\) is a proper exposed face of \(K\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible conic system either has a relative-interior feasible point or admits an adjoint exposing vector that is nontrivial on the cone and orthogonal to the right-hand side, but not both.

\(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Detecting Exposure Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict conic Farkas certificate detecting strongly separated infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). For the conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), any vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\]
is an infeasibility-detecting certificate, and
\[\{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing.\]
This certificate represents strict separation of \(b\) from \(A(K)\). A weakly infeasible system with \(b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K)\) need not admit such a strict certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier with dual-cone adjoint image and negative pairing with the right-hand side certifies infeasibility; weak infeasibility may escape this strict certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Iterated Face Exposure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial-reduction sequence for a feasible primal conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a closed convex cone \(K\), a linear map \(A\), and \(b\) with \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Initialize \(F_0=K\). At iteration \(i\), if \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i\neq\varnothing\), stop and output \(F_i\). Otherwise find \(y_i\) such that
\[z_i=A^*y_i\in F_i^*\setminus F_i^\perp,\qquad \langle b,y_i\rangle=0,\]
and update
\[F_{i+1}=F_i\cap z_i^\perp.\]
Each update produces a proper exposed face of \(F_i\) containing \(S\). In finite dimension the strictly descending sequence terminates after at most \(\dim(\operatorname{span}K)\) reductions, and its terminal face equals the minimal face containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly expose a proper feasible-set-containing face until relative strict feasibility holds. Finite-dimensional face dimension decreases each time, and the terminal cone is the minimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
An exposing multiplier is available whenever the current system lacks relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updates preserve \(S\), terminate finitely, and output \(F_{\min}=\operatorname{face}_K(S)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic stage count for exact iterated exposure of a feasible conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty conic system \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), its singularity degree is the minimum integer \(d\ge0\) for which there exist faces
\[
K=F_0\supsetneq F_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq F_d=\operatorname{face}_K(S)
\]
and valid exposing vectors \(z_i\in F_i^*\setminus F_i^\perp\) satisfying \(S\subseteq z_i^\perp\) and \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cap z_i^\perp\). It equals zero exactly when \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}K\ne\varnothing\). Every exact facial-reduction sequence has at least \(d\) reductions, some sequence has exactly \(d\), and
\[
d\le \dim(\operatorname{span}K)-\dim(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singularity degree is the minimum number of valid exposure steps needed to reach the minimal feasible face, with a dimension-drop upper bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimension.
\(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty.
A valid relative exposing vector is used at each reduction.

notation.meaning: Singularity degree of the feasible conic system.
Minimal face of K containing S.

knowledge_statements.title: Singularity Degree and Facial-Reduction Length
Partial Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Early-stopped facial reduction yielding a valid intermediate relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input \(K,A,b\), a target number \(t\geq0\), and a feasible set \(S=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\). Set \(F_0=K\). For \(i=0,\ldots,t-1\), either stop if \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i\neq\varnothing\), or choose an exposing certificate \(z_i=A^*y_i\in F_i^*\setminus F_i^\perp\) with \(\langle b,y_i\rangle=0\), and set \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cap z_i^\perp\). Output the last face \(F_r\), where \(r\leq t\). Then
\[F_{\min}\subseteq F_r\subseteq K,\qquad S=F_r\cap\{x:Ax=b\}.\]
Unless relative strict feasibility triggered stopping, \(F_r\) need not equal \(F_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stopping facial reduction early preserves the feasible set and yields an intermediate face containing the minimal face, but it may not restore relative strict feasibility.

children.title: Primal Facial Reduction
children.top_down_role: Face-reduction procedures driven by primal feasibility geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction applied to the primal variable cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), initialize \(F_0^P=K\). While no feasible point lies in \(\operatorname{ri}F_i^P\), select \(y_i\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[z_i^P=A^*y_i\in(F_i^P)^*\setminus(F_i^P)^\perp,\qquad \langle b,y_i\rangle=0,\]
and update
\[F_{i+1}^P=F_i^P\cap(z_i^P)^\perp.\]
Stop when \(\{x\in\operatorname{ri}F_i^P:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\), and output \(F_i^P\). Every update preserves all primal feasible points and strictly reduces the current face; with exact certificates in finite dimension, the output is the primal minimal face \(F_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal facial reduction repeatedly intersects the primal cone with certified exposing hyperplanes until the reduced primal system has a relative-interior feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
\(\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
Exact exposing certificates are selected at every nonterminal step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates finitely at \(F_P=\operatorname{face}_K\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\).

children.title: Dual Facial Reduction

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction applied to the cone of feasible dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, let \(c\in E\), and define the nonempty dual-slack set
\[D=K^*\cap\{c-A^*y:y\in\mathbb R^m\}.\]
Initialize \(F_0^D=K^*\). While \(D\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i^D=\varnothing\), choose \(x_i\in E\) satisfying
\[x_i\in(F_i^D)^*\setminus(F_i^D)^\perp,\qquad Ax_i=0,\qquad \langle c,x_i\rangle=0,\]
and update
\[F_{i+1}^D=F_i^D\cap x_i^\perp.\]
Each update is a proper exposed face of \(F_i^D\) containing \(D\). With an exact exposing vector available at every nonterminal step, finite-dimensional iteration terminates at
\[F_D=\operatorname{face}_{K^*}(D),\]
where \(D\cap\operatorname{ri}F_D\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual facial reduction uses vectors in the dual of the current slack face, satisfying the homogeneous affine constraints, to expose successively smaller faces containing every feasible dual slack until the minimal face is reached.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
\(A:E\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, \(c\in E\), and \(D=K^*\cap(c-\operatorname{range}A^*)\neq\varnothing\).
At every nonterminal step, an exact nontrivial exposing vector satisfying the displayed conditions is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure preserves \(D\), terminates finitely, and outputs \(F_D=\operatorname{face}_{K^*}(D)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Facial-Reduction Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled reduction of the primal and dual feasible-slack cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For primal and dual slack systems with initial faces \(F_0^p=K\) and \(F_0^d=K^*\), construct exposing vectors \(z_i^p\in (F_i^p)^*\) and \(z_i^d\in (F_i^d)^*\) that annihilate every feasible primal and dual slack, respectively. Update \[F_{i+1}^p=F_i^p\cap (z_i^p)^\perp,\qquad F_{i+1}^d=F_i^d\cap (z_i^d)^\perp.\] Stop each sequence when the corresponding feasible slacks meet the relative interior of its current face. The output faces are the minimal faces containing the respective feasible-slack sets; the two sequences may have different lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating valid exposing certificates shrink the primal and dual cones until each feasible-slack set satisfies relative-interior feasibility in its minimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
The primal and dual feasible-slack sets are nonempty.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Reduction Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction applied to only one member of a primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-dual conic pair is in a one-sided reduction regime when exactly one feasible-slack set fails relative-interior feasibility in its original cone. Thus either \(S_p\cap\operatorname{ri}K=\varnothing\) while \(S_d\cap\operatorname{ri}K^*\ne\varnothing\), or the reverse. Facial reduction is then performed only on the failing side, producing its minimal face by successive intersections with valid exposing hyperplanes; the other side retains its original cone and has reduction length zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only the primal or only the dual slack system requires facial reduction; the opposite side already has a relative-interior feasible slack.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space.
Both feasible-slack sets \(S_p\subseteq K\) and \(S_d\subseteq K^*\) are nonempty.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the container, but the exact primal-dual regime convention and zero-length assignment require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Exploiting Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction constrained to a known invariant or block-structured subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be a linear subspace containing all feasible slacks and preserved by the cone representation, such as a symmetry-fixed or block-diagonal subspace. Initialize \(F_0=K\). At iteration \(i\), find an exposing vector \(z_i\in (F_i)^*\cap L\) that annihilates the feasible-slack affine space, and set \(F_{i+1}=F_i\cap z_i^\perp\). Stop when the feasible slacks intersect \(\operatorname{ri}F_i\). When every required minimal-face exposure admits a representative in \(L\), this restricted procedure returns the same minimal face as unrestricted facial reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known symmetry or block structure restricts exposure searches to a smaller subspace without changing the resulting minimal face when that subspace contains sufficient certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(L\) contains the feasible-slack affine space.
Every face needed by the reduction has an exposing vector in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal face equals the minimal face of \(K\) containing all feasible slacks.

knowledge_statements.title: Singularity-Degree Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime classification used for local Hölder error-bound statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be the singularity degree of a feasible conic system, with \(d=0\) assigned to relative-interior feasible systems. The error-bound regimes are classified as \[d=0:\ \text{regular},\qquad d=1:\ \text{one-step singular},\qquad d\ge2:\ \text{multi-step singular}.\] For positive-semidefinite feasibility on bounded sets, this classification corresponds to the guaranteed Hölder exponents \(1\), \(1/2\), and at most the degree-sensitive exponent \(2^{-d}\), respectively. These are general guarantees rather than the necessarily sharp exponent of every individual instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singularity degree separates regular, one-step, and multi-step systems, with progressively weaker general Hölder error-bound guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The conic system is feasible and finite-dimensional.
For the exponent correspondence, the cone is positive semidefinite and the comparison set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degree-dependent guaranteed exponent is \(\alpha_d=2^{-d}\), with \(\alpha_0=1\).

children.title: Error-Bound Behavior
children.top_down_role: Local or global error-bound behavior near singular conic feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-Subregularity Form of a Local Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator formulation of the local conic-feasibility error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the set-valued mapping \(F(x)=(x-K)\times\{Ax-b\}\) and equip its product range with \(\|(u,v)\|_\Sigma=\|u\|+\|v\|\). Then \(F^{-1}(0)=S:=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x))=\operatorname{dist}(x,K)+\|Ax-b\|\). Thus \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x))\) locally at \(\bar x\in S\) is metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,0)\); replacing the right side by its \(\alpha\)-th power gives Hölder metric subregularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual error bound is metric subregularity, or Hölder metric subregularity, of the mapping that records cone and affine violations.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(A\) is linear and \(\bar x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual and metric-subregularity formulations are equivalent under the stated product norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Subregularity Form of a Local Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Error Bound Under Relative-Interior Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular error-bound regime for the intersection of a cone and an affine space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\). If \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}K\ne\varnothing\), then for every bounded set \(B\) there is \(\kappa_B>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,K\cap L)\le\kappa_B\bigl(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)+\operatorname{dist}(x,L)\bigr),\qquad x\in B.\] Consequently, because \(\operatorname{dist}(x,L)\le c\|Ax-b\|\) for a suitable constant \(c\) when \(L\ne\varnothing\), the standard cone-plus-affine residual admits a local Lipschitz error bound at every feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative-interior feasibility gives bounded linear regularity of the cone and affine space and hence a local exponent-one residual bound.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(L=\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(L\cap\operatorname{ri}K\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasibility system has a local Lipschitz error bound at every point of \(K\cap L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Error Bound Under Relative-Interior Feasibility
Error-Bound Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual-to-distance behavior near a feasible conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\) and define \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,K)+\lVert Ax-b\rVert\). A local Hölder error bound with exponent \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) holds at \(\bar x\in S\) if there are \(C,\delta>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le C\,r(x)^\alpha\] whenever \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le\delta\). Relative-interior feasibility generally supports \(\alpha=1\); facial degeneracy may leave only \(\alpha<1\), so distance can decay more slowly than the residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hölder error bound controls distance to feasibility by a power of cone and affine residuals; facial degeneracy can reduce the exponent below one.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(S\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Near \(\bar x\), feasibility distance is bounded by \(C r(x)^\alpha\) when the stated Hölder property holds.
