children.title: Degree-Sensitive Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Dependence of error-bound quality on singularity-degree regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-set Hölder error bound for nonempty semidefinite feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\mathbb S_+^n\cap\{X:\mathcal AX=b\}\ne\varnothing\) have singularity degree \(d\), where relative strict feasibility has degree zero. Define \[r(X)=\operatorname{dist}(X,\mathbb S_+^n)+\|\mathcal AX-b\|.\] For every bounded set \(B\subseteq\mathbb S^n\), there are constants \(C_B>0\) and \(\varepsilon_B>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(X,S)\le C_B r(X)^{2^{-d}}\] for every \(X\in B\) with \(r(X)\le\varepsilon_B\). The exponent is a general guarantee and need not be the largest valid exponent for the particular system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On bounded sets, nonempty SDP feasibility admits a local Hölder error bound whose generally guaranteed exponent is two to the power minus the singularity degree.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(S\ne\varnothing\).
Singularity degree assigns degree zero to relative strict feasibility.
The comparison set \(B\) is bounded.

children.title: Error-Bound Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Settings where useful error-bound behavior degrades or is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Hölder Threshold in the Degree-One Example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent threshold implied by the immutable two-by-two semidefinite failure family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the immutable family \(X_t\), one has \(r(X_t)=t^2\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(X_t,S)\ge\sqrt2\,t\). Hence, for every \(\alpha>1/2\), \[\frac{\operatorname{dist}(X_t,S)}{r(X_t)^\alpha}\ge\sqrt2\,t^{1-2\alpha}\longrightarrow\infty.\] Therefore no local Hölder error bound with exponent \(\alpha>1/2\) holds at \(X_0\) for this residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree-one PSD example rules out every Hölder exponent above one half, not only the Lipschitz exponent one.
assumptions_latex: \(X_t\), \(X_0\), \(S\), and \(r\) are those in the immutable failure example.
Distances use the Frobenius norm and \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No local estimate \(\operatorname{dist}(X,S)\le C r(X)^\alpha\) holds at \(X_0\) for any \(\alpha>1/2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Hölder Threshold in the Degree-One Example
Error-Bound Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A degree-one semidefinite system where every local Lipschitz error bound fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(S=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^2:X_{11}=0\}\), \(X_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\in S\), and \(X_t=\begin{pmatrix}t^2&t\\t&1\end{pmatrix}\) for \(t>0\). With \(r(X)=\operatorname{dist}(X,\mathbb S_+^2)+|X_{11}|\), one has \(r(X_t)=t^2\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(X_t,S)\ge\sqrt{2}\,t\) in Frobenius norm. Hence \(X_t\to X_0\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(X_t,S)/r(X_t)\to\infty\), so no local Lipschitz error bound holds at \(X_0\). The exposing matrix \(E_{11}\) reaches the minimal face in one step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degree-one semidefinite feasibility system has residual of order t squared but distance to feasibility of order t, so no local linear error bound holds at its limiting feasible point.
assumptions_latex: Distances to matrix sets use the Frobenius norm.
The parameter satisfies \(t>0\) and tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No constants \(C,\delta>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(X,S)\le C r(X)\) for every \(X\) with \(\lVert X-X_0\rVert_F\le\delta\).

The classification does not assert that all systems of the same degree have the same sharp exponent or modulus.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual-based Hölder conditioning of conic feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=K\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\), set \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,K)+\|Ax-b\|\). For \(\bar x\in S\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), define \[\kappa_\alpha(\bar x)=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{r(x)^\alpha}.\] The system is locally \(\alpha\)-Hölder conditioned at \(\bar x\) when \(\kappa_\alpha(\bar x)<\infty\). This is equivalent to a local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le C r(x)^\alpha\). The case \(\alpha=1\) is Lipschitz conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local conditioning compares distance to the feasible set with a power of the combined cone and affine residual.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(S\) is nonempty and \(\bar x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_\alpha(\bar x)<\infty\iff\text{a local Hölder error bound of exponent }\alpha\text{ holds at }\bar x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case Hölder conditioning consequence of the degree-sensitive SDP error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty semidefinite feasibility system of singularity degree \(d\), the degree-sensitive bounded-set error bound yields a Hölder conditioning guarantee with exponent \(2^{-d}\). Thus \(d=0\) yields a Lipschitz guarantee, \(d=1\) yields a square-root guarantee, and each additional reduction step halves this generally available exponent. This is a guaranteed exponent, not necessarily the largest exponent valid for the particular instance; singularity degree alone does not determine the sharp conditioning modulus.

This implication alone does not prove that every positive-degree instance lacks a Lipschitz error bound. Restriction to the minimal face restores relative strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Feasibility on the Minimal Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional feasibility statement for the minimal face of a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). Suppose \(S=\{x\in K:\mathcal A x=b\}\neq\varnothing\), and define \(F_{\min}\) as the intersection of all faces of \(K\) containing \(S\). Then there exists \(\bar x\in S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\). Hence the system \(\mathcal A x=b\), \(x\in F_{\min}\), is strictly feasible relative to \(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty conic feasible set contains a point in the relative interior of its minimal containing face, restoring relative strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Primal-Dual Pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual pairing formed in the linear span of a closed reduced face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(F\) be a closed face of \(K\). Set \(L=\operatorname{span}F\), let \(P_F:E\to L\) be the orthogonal projection, let \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) be linear, and take \(b\in Y\) and \(c\in E\). Pair the primal \(\inf\{\langle P_Fc,x\rangle:\mathcal A x=b,\ x\in F\}\) with the dual \(\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:y\in Y,\ P_F(c-\mathcal A^*y)\in F^*\}\), where \(F^*=\{s\in L:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in F\}\). If there exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) satisfying \(\mathcal A\bar x=b\) and the primal value is finite, then the primal and dual values coincide and the dual optimum is attained.

There exists \(\bar x\in\operatorname{ri}F\) with \(\mathcal A\bar x=b\), and the reduced primal value is finite.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coordinate reduction to the span of a face; no relaxation or approximation is introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(F\) be a face of a closed convex cone in \(E\), and set \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}F)\). Choose a linear isomorphism \(T:\mathbb R^k\to\operatorname{span}F\) and define \(K_F=T^{-1}(F)\). For a linear map \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) and \(b\in Y\), substitution \(x=Tz\) transforms \(\mathcal A x=b\), \(x\in F\), exactly into \((\mathcal A T)z=b\), \(z\in K_F\). The two substitutions are inverse bijections between the feasible sets. For every \(c\in E\), they also preserve the linear objective because \(\langle c,Tz\rangle=\langle T^*c,z\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinates on the span of the reduced face replace the original variable by one whose dimension equals that span while preserving feasibility and every linear objective.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(F\) is a face of a closed convex cone in \(E\).
\(T:\mathbb R^k\to\operatorname{span}F\) is a linear isomorphism, where \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}F)\).
\(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) is linear and \(b\in Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The substitution \(x=Tz\) gives an equivalent conic system in dimension \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}F)\) and preserves linear objectives under \(c\mapsto T^*c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Rank Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact removal of linearly dependent equality constraints after face-coordinate reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(B:\mathbb R^k\to Y\) be linear, and suppose \(Bz=b\) is feasible for \(b\in Y\). Set \(r=\operatorname{rank}B\). Choose a linear map \(P:Y\to\mathbb R^r\) whose restriction to \(\operatorname{range}B\) is injective, and output \(PBz=Pb\). Because feasibility gives \(b\in\operatorname{range}B\), the difference \(Bz-b\) belongs to \(\operatorname{range}B\); hence \(PBz=Pb\) if and only if \(Bz=b\). Moreover, \(PB\) has rank \(r\), so the output has exactly \(r\) independent scalar equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compress the equality map to a full-row-rank system with the same feasible set and exactly as many independent equations as the original map's rank.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, \(B:\mathbb R^k\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
The system \(Bz=b\) is feasible.
\(r=\operatorname{rank}B\), and \(P:Y\to\mathbb R^r\) is injective on \(\operatorname{range}B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The systems \(Bz=b\) and \(PBz=Pb\) are equivalent, and \(PB\) has rank \(r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Rank Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic tradeoff induced by restricting constraints to the span of the reduced face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces, let \(F\) be the reduced face in \(E\), and set \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}F)\). Choose a linear isomorphism \(T:\mathbb R^k\to\operatorname{span}F\), let \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) be linear, and define \(B=\mathcal A T\) and \(r=\operatorname{rank}B\). Then \(r\leq\min\{\operatorname{rank}\mathcal A,k\}\) and \(\dim\ker B=k-r\). The values \(k\), \(r\), and \(k-r\) are unchanged by a different choice of reduced coordinates or by invertible transformations of the equality rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After face reduction, the effective constraint rank cannot exceed either the original rank or reduced dimension, and reduced nullity equals dimension minus rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Representation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Irreducibility restricted to exact linear coordinate images and equivalent systems of linear equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces, let \(F\subseteq E\) be the minimal face containing the feasible set, set \(L=\operatorname{span}F\) and \(k=\dim L\), and let \(B:\mathbb R^k\to Y\) be the equality operator in reduced coordinates with rank \(r\). If a linear map \(Q:\mathbb R^q\to L\) and a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) satisfy \(Q(C)=F\), then \(q\geq k\), because \(F\) spans \(L\). If a feasible linear system \(Gz=d\) has the same solution set as \(Bz=b\), then \(\operatorname{rank}G=r\); consequently, any scalar-row description of that equivalent linear system contains at least \(r\) independent equations. Thus exact linear coordinates and equivalent linear equality descriptions cannot reduce these two sizes below \(k\) and \(r\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After reaching the span dimension of the minimal face and the rank of the reduced equality map, exact linear coordinates and equivalent linear equality systems cannot reduce those sizes further.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the minimal face containing the feasible set and \(k=\dim(\operatorname{span}F)\).
\(B:\mathbb R^k\to Y\) is the reduced equality operator and \(r=\operatorname{rank}B\).
Only exact linear coordinate images and equivalent systems of linear equalities are considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exact linear coordinate image covering \(F\) uses at least \(k\) coordinates, and every equivalent linear equality system has rank \(r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Subproblem Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity to the linear objective over a fixed reduced feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(\mu>0\). For every \(c\in E\), define \(x(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{\langle c,x\rangle+\tfrac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2\}\). The minimizer exists uniquely and satisfies \(x(c)=\operatorname{proj}_C(-c/\mu)\). Therefore, for all \(c_1,c_2\in E\), \(\|x(c_1)-x(c_2)\|\leq\mu^{-1}\|c_1-c_2\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic regularization makes the reduced minimizer unique and Lipschitz in the linear objective, with Lipschitz constant at most the reciprocal regularization strength.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
\(C\subseteq E\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniqueness and continuous objective sensitivity when quadratic regularization vanishes.

Thus the optimizer is nonunique at zero, and no exact optimizer selection agreeing with the unique optimizers for c\neq0 is continuous at zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence property for finite-dimensional semidefinite programs; the exact lifted formulation remains source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible semidefinite program \((P)\) with finite optimal value but without an ambient Slater point. A Ramana-type extended dual \((D_{\mathrm{ext}})\) augments the ordinary dual variables by a finite chain of semidefinite face-exposing variables that encodes reduction from the positive-semidefinite cone to the minimal face containing the primal feasible slacks. For the standard finite-dimensional construction, every feasible extended-dual objective is a valid primal lower bound, and \(\operatorname{val}(D_{\mathrm{ext}})=\operatorname{val}(P)\); moreover, \((D_{\mathrm{ext}})\) attains this value whenever \((P)\) has finite value.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Sequences as Dual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate of feasible-set containment in successively smaller exposed faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, let \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). Suppose \(S=\{x\in K:\mathcal A x=b\}\neq\varnothing\), and set \(F_0=K\). A facial-reduction certificate is a finite sequence \((y_i,z_i)_{i=1}^d\) such that \(y_i\in Y\), \(z_i=\mathcal A^*y_i\), \(z_i\in F_{i-1}^*=\{z\in E:\langle z,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }x\in F_{i-1}\}\), \(\langle b,y_i\rangle=0\), and \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap z_i^\perp\) is a proper face of \(F_{i-1}\). Every feasible point belongs to every \(F_i\). If \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_d\neq\varnothing\), then \(F_d\) is the minimal face of \(K\) containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjoint multipliers orthogonal to the right-hand side expose successively smaller faces containing every feasible point; terminal relative strict feasibility certifies the minimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
\(S=\{x\in K:\mathcal A x=b\}\neq\varnothing\).
For each \(i\), \(y_i\in Y\), \(z_i=\mathcal A^*y_i\in F_{i-1}^*\), \(\langle b,y_i\rangle=0\), and \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap z_i^\perp\) is a proper face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible point lies in every \(F_i\); if \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_d\neq\varnothing\), then \(F_d\) is the minimal face containing \(S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Expansions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact homogeneous conic lifts represented by a linear slice followed by a linear image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\), \(\widehat E\), and \(W\) be finite-dimensional vector spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a convex cone, and let \(\widehat K\subseteq\widehat E\) be a closed convex cone. An exact conic expansion of \(K\) consists of linear maps \(P:\widehat E\to E\) and \(H:\widehat E\to W\) satisfying \(K=P(\widehat K\cap\ker H)\). Equivalently, \(x\in K\) if and only if there exists \(z\in\widehat K\) such that \(Hz=0\) and \(Pz=x\). Replacing membership in \(K\) by these lifted constraints preserves the projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact conic expansion represents the original cone as the linear image of a homogeneous linear slice of a higher-dimensional closed convex cone.

\(K\subseteq E\) is a convex cone and \(\widehat K\subseteq\widehat E\) is a closed convex cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Dual Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation induced by an exact conic lift under lifted-space Slater feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\), \(\widehat E\), \(Y\), and \(W\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. Let \(K\subseteq E\) and \(\widehat K\subseteq\widehat E\) be convex cones with \(\widehat K\) closed, and let \(P:\widehat E\to E\) and \(H:\widehat E\to W\) be linear maps satisfying \(K=P(\widehat K\cap\ker H)\). For a linear map \(\mathcal A:E\to Y\), \(b\in Y\), and \(c\in E\), the primal problem \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:\mathcal A x=b,\ x\in K\}\) has the lifted form \(\inf\{\langle P^*c,z\rangle:\mathcal A Pz=b,\ Hz=0,\ z\in\widehat K\}\). Its conic dual is \(\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:y\in Y,\lambda\in W,\ P^*(c-\mathcal A^*y)-H^*\lambda\in\widehat K^*\}\). If there exists \(\bar z\in\operatorname{ri}\widehat K\) satisfying \(\mathcal A P\bar z=b\) and \(H\bar z=0\), and the lifted primal value is finite, then this dual attains the common primal-dual value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing an exact conic lift gives an extended dual; lifted Slater feasibility and a finite primal value ensure zero gap and dual attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(E\), \(\widehat E\), \(Y\), and \(W\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
\(K=P(\widehat K\cap\ker H)\), where \(\widehat K\subseteq\widehat E\) is a closed convex cone, \(P:\widehat E\to E\) is linear, and \(H:\widehat E\to W\) is linear.
\(\mathcal A:E\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(c\in E\).
There exists \(\bar z\in\operatorname{ri}\widehat K\) with \(\mathcal A P\bar z=b\) and \(H\bar z=0\), and the lifted primal value is finite.

Expansion-to-Dual Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lifting correspondence for a projected conic constraint and its extended dual multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(E,Z\) be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, let \(Q\subseteq E\times Z\) be a closed convex cone, and set \(K=\pi_E(Q)\). Then the constraint \(s\in K\) has the conic expansion
\[
s\in K\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z\in Z:\ (s,z)\in Q.
\]
For every \(u\in E\), membership in the dual cone is represented by
\[
u\in K^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (u,0)\in Q^*.
\]
Consequently, dualizing the lifted constraint over \(Q\) produces an extended-dual representation whose auxiliary variables are precisely the multipliers needed to certify membership of \((u,0)\) in \(Q^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection-based conic expansions correspond to dual certificates obtained by embedding a dual vector with zero auxiliary component in the lifted cone’s dual.

\(Q\subseteq E\times Z\) is a closed convex cone.

Nonrepresentability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary relative to a prescribed family of admissible conic expansions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a family \(\mathcal Q\) of closed convex cones allowed as lifts. A closed convex cone \(D\subseteq E\) is representable by this expansion family exactly when there exist \(Q\in\mathcal Q\), a finite-dimensional space \(Z\), and a linear map \(T:E\times Z\to E\) such that
\[
D=T(Q).
\]
Thus an extended-dual feasible cone \(D\) lies beyond the family’s representability boundary whenever no such \(Q\), \(Z\), and \(T\) exist. In that case no reformulation using only lifts from \(\mathcal Q\) can represent the extended-dual cone exactly, although approximations or a larger lift family may remain possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended dual is exactly representable by a chosen lift family only if its feasible cone is a linear image of an allowed cone.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Q\) is the fixed family of admissible closed convex lift cones.
All spaces are finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(D\neq T(Q)\) for every admissible \(Q\) and linear \(T\), then \(D\) has no exact \(\mathcal Q\)-expansion representation.

notation.meaning: Prescribed family of admissible lift cones.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Containment Correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness invariant for successive facial-reduction cuts containing every feasible slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let \(S\subseteq K\) be the feasible-slack set. Define \(F_0=K\). For \(i=1,\ldots,k\), suppose a certificate \(y_i\in F_{i-1}^*\) satisfies \(\langle y_i,s\rangle=0\) for every \(s\in S\), and define
\[
F_i=F_{i-1}\cap y_i^\perp.
\]
Then every \(F_i\) is a face of \(F_{i-1}\), and
\[
S\subseteq F_k\subseteq F_{k-1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_0=K.
\]
Hence the displayed directions form a directly checkable certificate that no feasible slack is removed by the reduction sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each dual exposing direction that annihilates all feasible slacks cuts to a smaller face while retaining the entire feasible-slack set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(S\subseteq K\).
\(y_i\in F_{i-1}^*\) and \(\langle y_i,s\rangle=0\) for all \(s\in S\).

notation.meaning: Face remaining after the ith reduction cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Identification Correctness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination criterion identifying the minimal cone face containing the feasible slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, let \(S\subseteq K\) be nonempty, and let \(F\unlhd K\) be a face satisfying \(S\subseteq F\). If
\[
S\cap\operatorname{ri}F\neq\varnothing,
\]
then \(F\) is the unique minimal face of \(K\) containing \(S\):
\[
F=\operatorname{face}_K(S):=\bigcap\{G\unlhd K:S\subseteq G\}.
\]
Accordingly, a face-containment certificate together with a feasible slack in \(\operatorname{ri}F\) certifies that facial reduction has reached the minimal face and should terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A containing face is the minimal feasible face once at least one feasible slack lies in its relative interior.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(S\subseteq K\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(E\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:X\to E\) be linear, let \(b\in E\), let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and define \(s(x)=b-Ax\) for \(x\in X\). Suppose \(F\unlhd K\) contains every slack \(s(x)\) for which \(s(x)\in K\). Then
\[
\{x\in X:s(x)\in K\}=\{x\in X:s(x)\in F\}.
\]
Therefore, for every objective function \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the problems
\[
\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ s(x)\in K\}\quad\text{and}\quad\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ s(x)\in F\}
\]
have identical feasible points, objective values at those points, infima, and primal minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing a cone by a face containing every feasible slack leaves the primal feasible set and optimization problem unchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed-Face Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limitation of facial-reduction steps based on a single exposing vector of the ambient cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let \(F\unlhd K\) be nonexposed, meaning that no \(y\in K^*\) satisfies
\[
F=K\cap y^\perp.
\]
Then no single facial-reduction certificate drawn from \(K^*\) can identify \(F\) exactly. Every valid one-step cut \(K\cap y^\perp\) that contains \(F\) is an exposed face strictly larger than \(F\). Thus algorithms restricted to ambient one-step exposure must use additional reductions inside intermediate faces or employ facial certificates richer than one supporting hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexposed face cannot be recovered by one ambient dual hyperplane; one-step exposure necessarily returns a strictly larger face.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
\(F\unlhd K\) is nonexposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is no \(y\in K^*\) such that \(F=K\cap y^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional distance characterization of weak infeasibility for an affine conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional normed space \(E\), and let \(H\subseteq E\) be a nonempty affine subspace. The conic system \(H\cap K\neq\varnothing\) is weakly infeasible when
\[
H\cap K=\varnothing
\quad\text{and}\quad
\operatorname{dist}(H,K):=\inf\{\|h-k\|:h\in H,\ k\in K\}=0.
\]
Equivalently, the system is infeasible, yet for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist \(h\in H\) and \(k\in K\) with \(\|h-k\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic system is weakly infeasible when its affine space misses the cone but has zero distance from it.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(H\subseteq E\) is a nonempty affine subspace.

notation.meaning: Infimal norm distance between H and K.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit affine PSD system with zero distance and no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(\mathbb S^2\), let
\[
H=\left\{X(t)=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{bmatrix}:t\in\mathbb R\right\},\qquad K=\mathbb S_+^2.
\]
No \(X(t)\) is positive semidefinite, because a positive-semidefinite matrix with zero \((1,1)\) entry must have zero first row and column. Nevertheless, the negative eigenvalue of \(X(t)\) equals \((t-\sqrt{t^2+4})/2\to0\) as \(t\to+\infty\). Hence \(H\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(H,K)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple affine line of two-by-two matrices is infeasible for the PSD cone but approaches it arbitrarily closely at infinity.
assumptions_latex: Distance is measured in any matrix norm on the finite-dimensional space \(\mathbb S^2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent attainable-image formulation for a primal conic equality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone and let \(A\) be linear. The system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), is weakly infeasible exactly when
\[
b\in\overline{A(K)}\setminus A(K).
\]
Equivalently, no \(x\in K\) satisfies \(Ax=b\), but there exists a sequence \(x_n\in K\) with \(Ax_n\to b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility means that the right-hand side is an unattained limit point of the conic image.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimension.
\(A\) is linear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Characterization of the Closure of a Conic Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure formula identifying unattained limit points of a linear image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space and let \(T\) be linear. Then \(T(K)\) is a convex cone and
\[
T(K)^*=\{y:T^*y\in K^*\},\qquad
\overline{T(K)}=T(K)^{**}=\{u:\langle u,y\rangle\ge0\ \text{for every }y\text{ with }T^*y\in K^*\}.
\]
Thus \(T(K)\) is nonclosed exactly when this bipolar set contains an element not attained as \(T(x)\) with \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closure of a conic image is the bipolar determined by dual vectors whose adjoint images lie in the dual cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimension.
\(T\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Characterization of the Closure of a Conic Image

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating general conic images from the polyhedral regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\) is a polyhedral cone in finite dimension and \(T\) is linear, then \(T(K)\) is a polyhedral cone and hence is closed. Consequently, nonclosed linear images require nonpolyhedral cone geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every linear image of a polyhedral cone is polyhedral and closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite-dimensional polyhedral cone.
\(T\) is linear.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Projection of the Rotated Quadratic Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit nonclosed image distinct from the deferred semidefinite-coordinate construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K=\{(u,v,w)\in\mathbb R^3:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge w^2\}
\]
and let \(T(u,v,w)=(u,w)\). If \(u=0\), membership in \(K\) forces \(w=0\); if \(u>0\), every \(w\in\mathbb R\) is attained by taking \(v=w^2/(2u)\). Therefore
\[
T(K)=\{(u,w):u>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},
\]
which is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the closed rotated quadratic cone onto its first and third coordinates gives an open half-plane together with the origin.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is the three-dimensional rotated quadratic cone.
\(T\) is the stated coordinate projection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent closedness test using the kernel saturation of the source cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space and let \(T\) be linear. Then
\[
T(K)\text{ is closed}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic image is closed exactly when the cone enlarged by the map's kernel is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone in finite dimension.
\(T\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(K)\text{ is closed}\iff K+\ker T\text{ is closed}.

Nonclosed Linear Images of Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional semidefinite example showing that a linear image of a closed cone need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and define the linear map \(T:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by
\[
T\!\left(\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\ b&c\end{bmatrix}\right)=(a,b).
\]
Positive semidefiniteness implies that \(a=0\) forces \(b=0\), while every pair with \(a>0\) is attained by choosing \(c\ge b^2/a\). Hence
\[
T(K)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
This image is not closed because \((1/n,1)\in T(K)\) converges to \((0,1)\notin T(K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a closed positive-semidefinite cone can produce a nonclosed set; a simple two-by-two example exhibits the failure.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S_+^2\) is the cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices.

Linear map retaining the first diagonal and off-diagonal entries.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Residual Does Not Imply Exact Face Containment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of residual-based approximate exposure for a fixed exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\), \(y=(1,0)\), and \(F=K\cap y^\perp=\{0\}\times\mathbb R_+\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the singleton \(S_\varepsilon=\{(\varepsilon/2,1)\}\subset K\) satisfies \(\sup_{s\in S_\varepsilon}\langle y,s\rangle=\varepsilon/2\le\varepsilon\), although \(S_\varepsilon\not\subset F\). Thus no positive pairing tolerance alone certifies exact containment in the nominally exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small positive exposure residuals can occur at points outside the exposed face.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, let \(S\subseteq K\) be nonempty, and let \(y_k\in K^*\) satisfy \(\|y_k\|=1\), \(y_k\to y\), and \[0\le\sup_{s\in S}\langle y_k,s\rangle\le\varepsilon_k,\qquad \varepsilon_k\downarrow0.\] Then \(y\in K^*\), \(\|y\|=1\), and \(S\subseteq K\cap y^\perp\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PSD Distance Bound from an Approximate Exposure Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite specialization converting a small exposure pairing into distance from the exposed face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=P^T=P^2\) be an orthogonal projector and \(F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:PXP=0\}\). If \(X\succeq0\), \(\operatorname{tr}X\le M\), and \(\langle P,X\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(PX)\le\varepsilon\), then \[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm F}(X,F)\le\sqrt{2M\varepsilon+\varepsilon^2}.\] Thus a positive residual does not prove exact containment, but under the trace bound it gives quantitative approximate containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a trace-bounded PSD matrix, a small projector exposure residual bounds Frobenius distance to the exposed PSD face.

\(X\succeq0\), \(\operatorname{tr}X\le M\), and \(\operatorname{tr}(PX)\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit residual convention for approximate exposure of a bounded feasible-slack set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, let nonempty bounded \(S\subseteq K\), and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). A vector \(y\) is a normalized \(\varepsilon\)-exposing vector for \(S\) when \(y\in K^*\), \(\|y\|=1\), and \(r_S(y):=\sup_{s\in S}\langle y,s\rangle\le\varepsilon\). Since all pairings are nonnegative, \(r_S(y)=0\) is equivalent to \(S\subseteq K\cap y^\perp\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), only approximate annihilation is certified unless an additional error bound converts residual to distance from the face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized dual-cone vector approximately exposes the feasible slacks when its pairing is uniformly small; only zero residual implies exact face containment without further error bounds.

\(S\subseteq K\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).

Approximate Face Exposure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based approximate exposure condition for a bounded set of feasible conic slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional inner-product space, let \(S\subseteq K\) be a nonempty bounded feasible-slack set, and let \(\varepsilon\ge0\). A vector \(y\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate exposing certificate for \(S\) when
\[
y\in K^*,\qquad \|y\|=1,\qquad
0\le \sup_{s\in S}\langle y,s\rangle\le\varepsilon.
\]
At \(\varepsilon=0\), the exposed face \(K\cap y^\perp\) contains \(S\). For positive tolerance the inequalities certify only approximate annihilation and, without an error bound, do not certify exact containment in that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized dual vector approximately exposes feasible slacks when its maximum pairing with them is at most the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
\(S\subseteq K\) is nonempty and bounded.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exclusionary and Strict-Superface Misidentifications Are Distinct
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthant example separating the two set-theoretic kinds of incorrect face selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^3\) and \(S=\{e_1\}\). Then \(F_{\min}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1\}\). The face \[F_{\mathrm{sup}}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2\}\] strictly contains \(F_{\min}\) while retaining \(S\). In contrast, \[F_{\mathrm{exc}}=\operatorname{cone}\{e_2\}\] is a face of \(K\) that excludes \(S\). Thus selecting a strict superface and selecting a face that removes feasible slacks are distinct misidentification modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One wrong orthant face can retain every feasible slack while being too large, whereas another can exclude the feasible slack.
assumptions_latex: \(e_1,e_2,e_3\) are the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{\min}\subsetneq F_{\mathrm{sup}}\text{ with }S\subseteq F_{\mathrm{sup}},\qquad S\nsubseteq F_{\mathrm{exc}}.

notation.meaning: selected strict superface of the minimal feasible face
selected face excluding the feasible slack

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Test for Correct Face Identification

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq K\) be nonempty and let \(\widehat F\unlhd K\) satisfy \(S\subseteq\widehat F\). children.title: Exposure-Tolerance Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization Is Necessary for Absolute Exposure Tolerances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling boundary for residual thresholds applied to exposing vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq K\), let \(0\ne y\in K^*\), and define \(r_S(y)=\sup_{s\in S}\langle y,s\rangle\). For every \(\alpha>0\), \(r_S(\alpha y)=\alpha r_S(y)\), while \(K\cap(\alpha y)^\perp=K\cap y^\perp\). Consequently, if \(r_S(y)>0\), then for every absolute tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) one can choose \(0<\alpha\le\varepsilon/r_S(y)\) so that \(r_S(\alpha y)\le\varepsilon\), without changing the candidate face. An absolute residual threshold is therefore meaningful only after fixing a normalization or replacing it by a scale-invariant relative residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling an exposing vector changes its absolute residual but not its face, so absolute tolerances require normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq K\).
The residual supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absolute residual acceptance is scale-dependent unless the exposing vector is normalized or a relative residual is used.

If the resulting pairing interval contains zero, this test does not resolve exact membership.

Exposure-Tolerance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Margin criterion separating stable and potentially unstable approximate exposure decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\in K^*\) satisfy \(\|y\|=1\), let \(F=K\cap y^\perp\), and fix \(\delta>0\). On
\[
B_\delta=\{x\in K:\|x\|\le1,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,F)\ge\delta\},
\]
assume the exposure margin \(\gamma_\delta:=\inf_{x\in B_\delta}\langle y,x\rangle\) is positive. If \(\|\widehat y-y\|\le\eta\), then every \(x\in B_\delta\) satisfies
\[
\langle\widehat y,x\rangle\ge\gamma_\delta-\eta.
\]
Thus thresholding at \(\varepsilon<\gamma_\delta-\eta\) cannot classify such points as belonging to the face. When \(\varepsilon+\eta\ge\gamma_\delta\), this margin guarantee disappears.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate exposure is stable when certificate error plus classification tolerance stays below the separation margin away from the face.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Superface Necessarily Retains Relative-Slater Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact regularity consequence of reducing only to a strict superface of the minimal feasible face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq K\) be nonempty, let \(F_{\min}=\operatorname{face}_K(S)\), and let \(\widehat F\unlhd K\) satisfy \(F_{\min}\subsetneq\widehat F\). Then \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}\widehat F=\varnothing\). Hence replacing \(K\) by the strict superface \(\widehat F\) preserves \(S\) but cannot establish relative strict feasibility; relative strict feasibility is recovered upon restriction to \(F_{\min}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reducing to a face strictly larger than the minimal feasible face preserves feasibility but necessarily leaves the system without a relative-interior feasible slack.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exclusionary Face Selection Can Change the Optimal Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic optimization example showing loss of primal equivalence after selecting a face that excludes feasible slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\{x_2:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\in\mathbb R_+^2\}.\] Its feasible-slack set is the segment \(S=\{(t,1-t):0\le t\le1\}\), its minimal cone face is \(\mathbb R_+^2\), and its optimal value is \(0\), attained at \(e_1\). If the cone is incorrectly replaced by the face \(\widehat F=\operatorname{cone}\{e_2\}\), then the reduced model has the single feasible point \(e_2\) and optimal value \(1\). Thus an exclusionary face can preserve nonemptiness while removing an optimizer and changing the optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting an orthant program to a wrongly selected face can retain feasibility yet remove the original optimizer and change the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimization of \(x_2\).
\(e_1,e_2\) are the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Under-Reduction Does Not Imply a Duality Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that failure to reach the minimal face does not itself force an adverse duality status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\{0:x_1=1,\ x_2=0,\ x\in\mathbb R_+^2\}.\] Its feasible set is \(\{e_1\}\), with minimal cone face \(\operatorname{cone}\{e_1\}\). If no reduction is performed, \(\widehat F=\mathbb R_+^2\) is a strict superface and the feasible set misses \(\operatorname{ri}\widehat F\). Nevertheless, the dual \[\max\{y_1:(y_1,y_2)+s=0,\ s\in\mathbb R_+^2\}\] has attained value \(0\), equal to the attained primal value. Thus incomplete facial reduction alone implies neither a positive duality gap nor nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A system can remain on the relative boundary of an oversized face while retaining attained primal and dual optima with zero gap.
assumptions_latex: The nonnegative orthant is self-dual.
The displayed equality-form primal-dual convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat F\supsetneq F_{\min}\) and relative Slater fails in \(\widehat F\), yet \(v_P=v_D=0\) and both optima are attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Under-Reduction Does Not Imply a Duality Gap
Misidentification Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinct primal consequences of selecting a face above or below the minimal feasible face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the original feasible-slack set, let \(F_{\min}=\operatorname{face}_K(S)\), and replace \(K\) by a selected face \(\widehat F\unlhd K\). If \(F_{\min}\subsetneq\widehat F\), then the primal feasible set is unchanged, but the reduced system need not possess a slack in \(\operatorname{ri}\widehat F\); strict feasibility and regularized duality may therefore remain unavailable. If \(S\nsubseteq\widehat F\), then at least one original feasible point is removed, so feasibility status, the optimal value, and the minimizer set may change. Hence under-reduction is incomplete, whereas over-reduction is not primal-equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing too large a face can preserve degeneracy; choosing a face that is too small can alter feasibility and optimal solutions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{v^1,\ldots,v^p\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and let \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(R\) may be empty. Using \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\), define
\[
G(V,R)=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i v^i+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j r^j:\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p,\ \mu\in\mathbb R_+^q,\ \sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
G(V,R)=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).
\]
Thus each represented point is a convex combination of point generators plus a nonnegative combination of recession generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The represented set consists exactly of convex combinations of point generators plus nonnegative combinations of ray generators; an empty ray family contributes only the zero vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a polyhedron if and only if there exist finite sets \(V\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(V\neq\varnothing\), and \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\). The ray set may be empty, with \(\operatorname{cone}(\varnothing)=\{0\}\). In particular, \(P\) is a polytope if and only if it admits such a representation without nonzero recession rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set is polyhedral exactly when it has a finite representation by convex combinations of points plus nonnegative combinations of rays; bounded polyhedra need no nonzero rays.

children.title: Recession Structure
children.top_down_role: Recession cones and unbounded directions associated with conic generation sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent recession tests, lineality, and the boundedness criterion for closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Its recession cone is
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{d:x+td\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\ge0\}.
\]
For any fixed \(x_0\in C\), equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{d:x_0+td\in C\text{ for every }t\ge0\}.
\]
It is a closed convex cone, and
\[
C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{0\}.
\]
Its lineality space is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(C)=\operatorname{rec}(C)\cap(-\operatorname{rec}(C)).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex set, recession can be tested from any one base point; the recession set is a closed convex cone, is trivial exactly for bounded sets, and its symmetric part is the lineality space.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The one-point and all-points recession definitions agree; \(\operatorname{rec}(C)\) is a closed convex cone, \(C\) is bounded iff it is trivial, and its symmetric part is \(\operatorname{lin}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Recession-Cone Structure
Recession Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession cone of a compact convex base plus a closed cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone. For \(C=B+K\), define
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:x+td\in C\text{ for every }x\in C\text{ and }t\geq0\}.
\]
Then \(C\) is closed and convex, and
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=K.
\]
Consequently, in a representation \(C=\operatorname{conv}(V)+K\) with finite nonempty \(V\), all unbounded directions are determined by \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a closed convex cone to a compact convex base produces a closed convex set whose recession cone is exactly the added cone.

children.title: Extreme-Ray Representations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic criterion for a ray to be extreme in a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone and \(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\). The ray \(R=\mathbb R_+r\) is an extreme ray of \(K\) if and only if
\[
x,y\in K,\quad x+y\in R\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x,y\in R.
\]
Equivalently, if \(r=x+y\) with \(x,y\in K\), then \(x\) and \(y\) are nonnegative scalar multiples of \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray is extreme when every conic decomposition of a vector on it remains on that same ray.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a convex cone.
\(r\in K\setminus\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb R_+r\) is extreme exactly when every conic decomposition of a point on it remains within that ray.

notation.meaning: ray generated by the nonzero vector r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why extreme rays alone do not represent cones containing lines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone with nontrivial lineality space \(L=K\cap(-K)\). No nonzero vector of \(L\) generates an extreme ray of \(K\). In particular, a nonzero linear subspace, regarded as a cone, has no extreme rays and cannot be generated by extreme rays. A general polyhedral-cone representation must account separately for lineality and for rays of an associated pointed quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extreme rays alone cannot represent nontrivial lineality; a general cone representation must separately account for its subspace component.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No nonzero \(r\in K\cap(-K)\) generates an extreme ray of \(K\).

Extreme-Ray Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite extreme-ray generation of pointed polyhedral cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a pointed polyhedral cone. It has finitely many extreme rays. If \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\) contain one nonzero representative from each extreme ray, then
\[
K=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_jr^j:\mu\in\mathbb R_+^q\right\}.
\]
Moreover, any finite set \(R\subseteq K\) satisfying \(K=\operatorname{cone}(R)\) must contain a vector on every extreme ray of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointed polyhedral cone is generated by representatives of its finitely many extreme rays, and every finite exact generator set meets each extreme ray.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a pointed polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=\operatorname{cone}\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\), with one representative required on every extreme ray.

children.title: Nonextreme Ray Generators
children.top_down_role: Redundant or aggregated ray families used to represent recession structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal and Separating Certificates for Generator Redundancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite certificates that a ray is removable or indispensable relative to the remaining generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and fix \(j\). The generator \(r^j\) is redundant exactly when there are coefficients \(\mu_k\ge0\), \(k\ne j\), satisfying
\[
r^j=\sum_{k\ne j}\mu_k r^k.
\]
If no such coefficients exist, then, because \(\operatorname{cone}(R\setminus\{r^j\})\) is a closed polyhedral cone, there is a vector \(y\) such that
\[
\langle y,r^k\rangle\ge0\quad(k\ne j),
\qquad
\langle y,r^j\rangle<0.
\]
The first system certifies safe deletion; the second certifies that deleting \(r^j\) strictly changes the generated cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative coefficients certify that a generator is redundant, while a separating vector certifies that it is indispensable relative to the remaining finite family.
assumptions_latex: \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(r^j\in\operatorname{cone}(R\setminus\{r^j\})\) has a nonnegative coefficient certificate, or a separating vector certifies its nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal and Separating Certificates for Generator Redundancy

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a convex cone.
\(R\subseteq K\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactness is equivalent to \(\operatorname{cone}(R)=K\), and any generator in the conic hull of the remaining generators can be removed without changing the generated cone.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: immediate finite-dimensional conic-hull redundancy criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recession generation with redundant or nonextreme rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a convex cone and let \(R=\{r^1,\ldots,r^q\}\subseteq K\). The generator representation is exact precisely when
\[
\operatorname{cone}(R)=K.
\]
The vectors in \(R\) need not generate extreme rays. If \(r^j\in\operatorname{cone}(R\setminus\{r^j\})\), then \(r^j\) is redundant and
\[
\operatorname{cone}(R)=\operatorname{cone}(R\setminus\{r^j\}).
\]
If \(K\) is pointed and polyhedral and \(R\) generates \(K\), deleting every generator lying on one extreme ray of \(K\) destroys exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonextreme rays are valid generators when their conic hull is the target cone, and any generator produced conically by the others is redundant. For a pointed polyhedral cone, an exact finite generator family must retain a generator on every extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonextreme Ray Generators

children.title: Incomplete-Ray Boundary
children.top_down_role: Generation failures caused by missing recession directions or insufficient ray families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of exact generation even when available rays generate a dense subcone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\) and
\[
R=\{(1,t):t>0\}\cup\{(t,1):t>0\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{cone}(R)=\{0\}\cup\mathbb R_{++}^2\subsetneq K,
\qquad
\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cone}(R))=K.
\]
Thus arbitrarily accurate approximation of every recession direction does not make the ray representation exact; the boundary rays remain unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A ray family can generate a dense proper subcone, so closure-level completeness does not imply exact ray completeness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by omitting an indispensable extreme ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e_1=(1,0)\), \(e_2=(0,1)\), and \(K=\mathbb R_+^2=\operatorname{cone}\{e_1,e_2\}\). If the available ray family is \(R=\{e_1\}\), define \(\widehat K=\operatorname{cone}(R)\). Then
\[
\widehat K=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\{(t,0):t\geq0\}\subsetneq K,
\qquad e_2\notin\widehat K.
\]
Hence a master representation using \(R\) cannot represent points whose recession component has positive second coordinate. More generally, if a finite generator family for a pointed polyhedral cone contains no vector on one of the cone's extreme rays, its generated cone is a strict subset of the target cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Omitting an extreme-ray direction can strictly shrink the generated recession cone; the nonnegative quadrant generated only by its first axis misses its second axis.

Lifted Atomic Conic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenized conic lift of finite convex combinations of atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and define the homogenized atomic cone
\[
K_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{cone}\{(a,1):a\in\mathcal A\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}.
\]
Then the finite convex hull of the atoms has the lifted conic representation
\[
\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:(x,1)\in K_{\mathcal A}\}.
\]
Indeed, the last-coordinate equation normalizes the nonnegative conic coefficients to sum to one. If \(K_{\mathcal A}\) is replaced by its closure, the slice may represent additional limit points unless closure commutes with the height-one slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenize each atom by appending one; the height-one slice of their conic hull is exactly their finite convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-inequality interpretation of the dual homogenized atomic cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(K_{\mathcal A}=\operatorname{cone}\{(a,1):a\in\mathcal A\}\),
\[
K_{\mathcal A}^*=\{(y,\tau)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\langle y,a\rangle+\tau\ge0\ \text{for every }a\in\mathcal A\}.
\]
Equivalently, its elements are precisely the affine functions nonnegative on every atom, hence on \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual homogenized atomic cone consists exactly of affine functions that are nonnegative on every atom.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest closed convex set containing a generator set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its closed convex hull is
\[
\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\bigcap\{C\subseteq\mathbb R^n:C\text{ is closed and convex, and }S\subseteq C\}.
\]
Thus it is the unique smallest closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^n\) containing \(S\). For \(S=\varnothing\), both the convex hull and closed convex hull are taken to be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is the closure of the convex hull, equivalently the smallest closed convex set containing the generators.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of linear infima and suprema on a set, its convex hull, and its closed convex hull, without an attainment claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), as extended-real equalities,
\[
\inf_{s\in S}c^\top s=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)}c^\top x,
\]
and analogously for suprema. Thus convexification and closure preserve linear optimal values, although they may change attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear optimal values are unchanged by convexification and closure, but attainment can change.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(c\in\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of the closed convex hull as the intersection of all closed halfspaces valid for the generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[
\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)=\bigcap_{a\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^\top x\leq\sup_{s\in S}a^\top s\right\},
\]
using extended-real support values: a right-hand side \(+\infty\) imposes no restriction, while \(\sup\varnothing=-\infty\) makes the represented intersection empty. Equivalently, a point belongs to the closed convex hull exactly when it satisfies every closed affine-halfspace inequality valid on \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull is the intersection of all closed halfspaces containing the generator set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
Extended-real support values are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\iff a^\top x\leq\sup_{s\in S}a^\top s\ \forall a\in\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). For nonempty \(S\), define its convex generation closure by
\[
\mathcal G(S)=\operatorname{cl}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i s_i:k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1},\ s_i\in S,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal G(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S)).
\]
Equivalently, \(x\in\mathcal G(S)\) precisely when a sequence of finite convex combinations of elements of \(S\) converges to \(x\). Define \(\mathcal G(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generation closure consists of all finite convex combinations of generators and all Euclidean limits of sequences of such combinations; the empty set has empty generation closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generation Closure Is a Closure Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and idempotence properties of convex generation closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\mathcal G(S)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\), with \(\mathcal G(\varnothing)=\varnothing\). Then
\[
S\subseteq\mathcal G(S),\qquad S\subseteq T\Longrightarrow\mathcal G(S)\subseteq\mathcal G(T),\qquad \mathcal G(\mathcal G(S))=\mathcal G(S).
\]
Moreover, \(\mathcal G(S)\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex generation closure is extensive, monotone, and idempotent, and its values are closed convex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(S,T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathcal G(S)\), \(S\subseteq T\Rightarrow\mathcal G(S)\subseteq\mathcal G(T)\), and \(\mathcal G(\mathcal G(S))=\mathcal G(S)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Generation Closure Is a Closure Operator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional support bound for generated convex combinations and their limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty. Every \(x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a convex combination of at most \(n+1\) points of \(S\). Consequently,
\[
x\in\mathcal G(S)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists\,(x_m),\ x_m\to x,\quad
x_m=\sum_{i=1}^{k_m}\lambda_{mi}s_{mi},\quad k_m\le n+1,
\]
where \(s_{mi}\in S\), \(\lambda_{mi}\ge0\), and \(\sum_i\lambda_{mi}=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each finitely generated point needs at most n+1 generators, and every point of the generation closure is a limit of combinations having that uniform support bound.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every point of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) uses at most \(n+1\) generators, and every point of \(\mathcal G(S)\) is a limit of such combinations.

notation.meaning: number of generators in the m-th convex combination

For every nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),

\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)
=\mathcal G(S)
=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists\,(x_m)_{m\geq1}\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ such that }x_m\to x\right\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization consequence of replacing a convex hull by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(\overline C=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)\). For every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\inf_{x\in C}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in\overline C}c^\top x\). If this common value is finite, the problem over \(\overline C\) attains it, and every minimizer over \(\overline C\) lies in \(\overline C\setminus C\), then the problem over \(C\) has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a convex hull preserves every linear infimum but can supply all optimizers, leaving the unclosed problem nonattained.
assumptions_latex: The common linear infimum is finite.
The problem over \(\overline C\) attains its minimum.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_C c^\top x=\min_{\overline C}c^\top x\) and \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}c^\top x=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary at which finite convex generation fails to equal the closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a closure gap occurs exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed:
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(S)
\iff
\exists\,x_k\in\operatorname{conv}(S),\ \bar x\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ with }x_k\to\bar x.
\]
Every point in the difference is a limit of finite convex combinations but has no finite convex-combination representation from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closure gap exists exactly when the finite convex hull is nonclosed, equivalently when finite mixtures converge to an unrepresentable limit point.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).

Closure-Gap Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonclosed generation can omit limit points and lose attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert x\rVert_2<1\}\). Since \(S\) is convex,
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)=S
\quad\text{but}\quad
\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert x\rVert_2\leq1\}.
\]
Therefore every unit vector belongs to the closed generated hull but has no finite convex representation by elements of \(S\). For any unit vector \(c\), the infimum of \(c^Tx\) over \(S\) equals \(-1\), but it is attained only after closure, at \(-c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open unit ball equals its convex hull but not its closed convex hull; closure adds the unit sphere and can restore objective attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(\lVert c\rVert_2=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\), and linear optimization over \(S\) need not attain its infimum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-one initialization for an equality-coupled restricted conic master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A_R\in\mathbb R^{m\times p}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), initialize the restricted master by solving
\[
\min_{\lambda,u^+,u^-}\ \mathbf 1^\top(u^++u^-)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
A_R\lambda+u^+-u^-=b,
\quad \lambda\in\mathbb R_+^p,
\quad u^+,u^-\in\mathbb R_+^m.
\]
A feasible initial point is \(\lambda=0\), \(u_i^+=\max\{b_i,0\}\), and \(u_i^-=\max\{-b_i,0\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Solve the phase-one problem to optimality. If its optimal value is zero, output the resulting \(\lambda\), which satisfies \(A_R\lambda=b\) and \(\lambda\geq0\); otherwise report that the current restricted column family admits no feasible master point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add positive and negative artificial columns and minimize their total weight. The phase-one problem is always feasible, and the current restricted master is feasible exactly when its optimal artificial weight is zero.

Blockwise Exact Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact point-generator pricing for every bounded convex block at a fixed master-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a master linking dual vector \(\pi\), block convexity multipliers \(\alpha_i\), and block oracles for \(X_i\). For every block \(i\), solve globally
\[
q_i^*=\min_{x\in X_i}\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\bigr)^{\mathsf T}x-\alpha_i,
\]
and retain an optimizer \(x_i^*\). If \(q_i^*<0\), add \(x_i^*\) as an improving point generator for block \(i\). If \(q_i^*\ge0\) for every block, return a no-improving-point certificate for the current dual vector. The procedure is exact only when each reported value is the global block minimum, rather than a local or heuristic value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided block pricing bounds that make an inexact oracle decision mathematically verifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For block \(i\), let \(q_i^*\) be its exact minimum reduced cost. A certified inexact oracle returns a feasible generator \(\hat x_i\), its reduced cost \(U_i\), and a valid lower bound \(L_i\) satisfying
\[
L_i\le q_i^*\le U_i
=\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\hat x_i-\alpha_i.
\]
If \(U_i<0\), then \(\hat x_i\) is a certified improving generator. If \(L_i\ge0\), no improving generator exists in that block. Otherwise the oracle is inconclusive; the certified absolute pricing error is at most \(U_i-L_i\), and additional oracle work is required before declaring blockwise optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible column gives an upper pricing bound and a relaxation gives a lower bound. Their signs certify improvement or nonexistence; overlapping zero is inconclusive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_i\ne\varnothing\) be closed and convex in finite dimensions, let \(R_i=\operatorname{rec}(X_i)\), and set \(a_i=c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\). If \(d\in R_i\) satisfies \(a_i^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(\inf_{x\in X_i}a_i^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\). Positive rescaling preserves this property, so any norm may normalize \(d\ne0\). The converse holds when \(X_i\) is polyhedral, but not for every closed convex set: for \(X=\{(x,y):y\ge x^2\}\) and \(a=(1,0)\), \(\inf_{z\in X}a^{\mathsf T}z=-\infty\), while \(\operatorname{rec}(X)=\{(0,t):t\ge0\}\) contains no direction with \(a^{\mathsf T}d<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative recession slope always gives unbounded pricing and can be normalized. Unbounded pricing implies such a ray for polyhedral blocks, but not for arbitrary closed convex blocks.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\ne\varnothing\) is closed and convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
The converse assertion additionally assumes that \(X_i\) is polyhedral.

knowledge_statements.title: Ray-Slope Implication and Converse Boundary
Ray Pricing for Unbounded Blocks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pricing recession directions that generate master rays rather than convex-combination point columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For block \(X_i\) with recession cone \(R_i=\operatorname{rec}(X_i)\), input a linking dual vector \(\pi\) and solve a normalized ray problem
\[
\eta_i^*=\min\left\{\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\bigr)^{\mathsf T}d:
 d\in R_i,\ \lVert d\rVert=1\right\}.
\]
If \(\eta_i^*<0\), add an optimizing direction \(d_i^*\) to the master as a nonnegative ray variable, contributing \(A_id_i^*\) to the linking equations and \(c_i^{\mathsf T}d_i^*\) to the objective, but contributing nothing to the block convexity equation. If no negative direction exists, point pricing remains responsible for affine offsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search the normalized recession cone for a negative-reduced-cost direction. Add such a direction as a ray variable without a coefficient in the block convexity equation.
assumptions_latex: \(X_i\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The normalization has a minimizer whenever \(R_i\) contains a nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_i^*<0\Rightarrow d_i^*\) is an improving master ray with zero convexity-row coefficient.

children.title: Parallel Pricing
children.top_down_role: Concurrent pricing across blocks, scenarios, or oracle partitions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal work and critical-path bounds for independent block pricing from one frozen dual snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_i^k\) be block \(i\)'s pricing time at synchronous snapshot \(k\). Excluding communication, scheduling, and master-solve overhead, serial evaluation takes \(\sum_{i=1}^B T_i^k\), while simultaneous execution with one worker per block takes \(\max_{1\le i\le B}T_i^k\). Hence the ideal speedup is \(\sum_iT_i^k/\max_iT_i^k\le B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ideal parallel pricing latency is the slowest block time; load imbalance limits speedup.
assumptions_latex: All pricing problems use the same frozen dual snapshot.
One dedicated worker is available per block.

knowledge_statements.title: Ideal Synchronous Pricing Latency
Parallel Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous simultaneous block pricing from one common master-dual snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At major iteration \(k\), solve the restricted master and freeze the dual snapshot \((\pi^k,\alpha_1^k,\ldots,\alpha_B^k)\). Dispatch all block pricing problems simultaneously:
\[
q_i^k=\min_{x\in X_i}\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi^k\bigr)^{\mathsf T}x-\alpha_i^k.
\]
Wait until every required worker returns a certified result. Add, in one batch, each returned generator having negative reduced cost, optionally after duplicate removal, and then re-solve the master. Stop when every exact value or certified lower bound is nonnegative. Because all workers use the same snapshot, their reduced costs are directly valid for the same restricted-master dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Freeze one dual solution, price all blocks concurrently, batch the improving columns, and re-solve. Terminate only when every block supplies a nonnegative exact value or lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Workers receive the same dual snapshot at each major iteration.
Every block eventually returns an exact result or a valid pricing bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The batch contains precisely the returned generators certified improving at snapshot \(k\).

children.title: Asynchronous Pricing

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Pricing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven pricing in which workers return columns without a global synchronization barrier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The coordinator maintains master version \(k\) and broadcasts dual snapshots to available block workers. Worker \(i\) prices using its received version \(s_i\), returns a generator, its reduced cost, and \(s_i\), then immediately accepts a newer assignment. Upon receipt, the coordinator validates the result against the current dual data, inserts it if it remains improving, and may re-solve the master without waiting for other blocks. Termination is allowed only after every block has been priced against a common sufficiently recent version and has returned a nonnegative exact value or valid lower bound. Fair scheduling and bounded communication delay prevent a block from being ignored indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers price and return columns without barriers. The coordinator validates each result at the current dual solution; termination still requires recent nonnegative certificates from every block.
assumptions_latex: Every block is scheduled infinitely often unless termination occurs.
Communication and computation delays are finite, and stale results are revalidated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only generators certified improving for the current master version are inserted; termination requires coverage of all blocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sign Reversal Under Stale Dual Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimal example showing that stale negative reduced cost need not remain negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take one scalar generator with \(A_ix=1\), \(c_i=0\), and \(\alpha_i^s=\alpha_i^k=0\). For \(\pi^s=1\), \(r_i^s(x)=-1<0\); for \(\pi^k=-1\), \(r_i^k(x)=1>0\). Thus stale negativity alone is not a current improvement certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the master multiplier can reverse a column's reduced-cost sign.
assumptions_latex: \(r_i^t(x)=(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi^t)^{\mathsf T}x-\alpha_i^t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sign Reversal Under Stale Dual Data
Stale Pricing Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A margin test ensuring that a column priced at an old dual vector still improves at the current vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a point generator \(x\in X_i\) was priced at stale dual data \((\pi^s,\alpha_i^s)\), giving reduced cost \(r_i^s(x)\). At current data \((\pi^k,\alpha_i^k)\),
\[
\left|r_i^k(x)-r_i^s(x)\right|
\le \lVert A_ix\rVert_*\lVert\pi^k-\pi^s\rVert
   +|\alpha_i^k-\alpha_i^s|.
\]
Consequently, the stale result remains a certified improving column if
\[
r_i^s(x)+\lVert A_ix\rVert_*\lVert\pi^k-\pi^s\rVert
+|\alpha_i^k-\alpha_i^s|<0.
\]
Failure of this test does not show nonimprovement; it requires direct reevaluation at the current dual data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound reduced-cost drift by dual drift. A stale column is safely accepted only when its old negative margin exceeds that bound; otherwise reevaluate it.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual norms are paired by Hölder's inequality.
Reduced cost is \(r_i^t(x)=(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi^t)^{\mathsf T}x-\alpha_i^t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed strict margin condition implies \(r_i^k(x)<0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Pricing Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Versioned coordinator-worker protocol for distributed block pricing and master updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a coordinator with restricted master \(M^0\) and version \(k=0\). Repeatedly: solve \(M^k\); broadcast the versioned dual data and block assignments; let each worker return a generator or a certified lower bound together with its block and version; verify feasibility, recompute or bound current reduced cost, and discard duplicates; insert every currently certified improving generator; then increment \(k\) after each master re-solve. A block certificate is invalidated whenever its dual version falls outside the accepted staleness rule. Output the current master solution only when every block has a valid nonnegative pricing certificate for the termination version.

knowledge_statements.title: Improving-Generator Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible point or ray whose verified reduced cost is strictly negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a dual-feasible restricted-master solution with linking multiplier \(\pi\) and block convexity multiplier \(\alpha_i\), a point \(x\in X_i\) is an improving-generator certificate when
\[
r_i(x)=\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\bigr)^{\mathsf T}x-\alpha_i<0.
\]
The certificate consists of \(x\), evidence that \(x\in X_i\), and the reproducible reduced-cost calculation. For a recession direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(X_i)\), the corresponding certificate is
\[
r_i^{\mathrm{ray}}(d)=\bigl(c_i-A_i^{\mathsf T}\pi\bigr)^{\mathsf T}d<0,
\]
with no \(\alpha_i\) term because a ray has zero coefficient in the convexity equation. Either certificate identifies a column that violates the associated dual constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible block point or recession direction with verified negative reduced cost certifies an improving column and a violated dual constraint.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master is a minimization problem and its displayed dual variables are feasible.
Membership in the block or its recession cone is verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_i(x)<0\) or \(r_i^{\mathrm{ray}}(d)<0\) certifies an improving generator for block \(i\).
